Delhi Police has intensified its investigation into the alleged violence during the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)-led protest in the national capital, with investigators set to analyse CCTV footage, drone videos, mobile phone recordings and other digital evidence to identify those involved.

According to police sources, multiple investigation teams have been formed to examine the available footage and identify individuals accused of attacking security personnel and damaging public property during the protest.

Officials are also trying to determine whether “outsiders” and “habitual offenders” infiltrated the demonstrations and contributed to the violence, beyond those already identified at the protest site.

Mobile Internet Suspended Near Jantar Mantar

Meanwhile, the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) has ordered the suspension of mobile internet services within a 1.5-kilometre radius of Jantar Mantar from 4 pm to midnight on Thursday.

The temporary restriction comes as security agencies continue monitoring the protest site and investigate the incidents of violence reported during the demonstrations over the alleged NEET paper leak.

body:
Amid the ongoing student protests, Delhi Police on Thursday said it had identified and blocked around 480 Pakistan-based social media handles allegedly involved in spreading fake and misleading content related to the agitation.

In a video message, the police said the accounts were circulating misinformation to provoke people and distract students. It claimed that many of the identified handles were the same ones that had been active during Operation Sindoor.

The @Cockroachisback protest appears to have lost sight of its original objective and is now moving without a clear direction. (#NEETExamIssue #CJP) For the first 20 days, the protest remained peaceful, but it received very little media attention. It was only after the clash between the Delhi Police and CJP that the media began giving it significant coverage. Since then, the movement seems to have expanded beyond its initial purpose.

The original demands were for the Union Government to take accountability for the alleged NEET question paper leak and for Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign. However, the protest has since broadened to include demands such as Prime Minister Modi's resignation, the release of Umar Khalid, and the restoration of Article 370. These issues are unrelated to the core objective with which the protest began.

A similar shift can be seen in Tamilnadu. Initially, CJP's protests were peaceful and focused on the NEET issue. But after inviting several Instagram influencers who are perceived to lean towards the DMK, the narrative increasingly shifted towards criticizing the TVK government rather than focusing on the alleged NEET paper leak. There is also a fundamental difference in objectives. In Tamilnadu, many political parties, including TVK, seek the complete abolition of NEET. CJP, however, has primarily been demanding that NEET be conducted fairly and transparently, and that the Union Government be held accountable whenever irregularities or paper leaks occur. Mixing unrelated political demands with that objective risks diluting the movement's original purpose. 

It appeared that the Aam Aadmi Party was trying to capitalize on the CJP protest after losing power in Delhi to the BJP. However, Rahul Gandhi's protest outside the Prime Minister's residence seems to have changed the political dynamics. Since then, AAP's approach appears to have shifted, and some of its leaders and supporters have also begun criticizing the protestors and CJP, rather than backing the movement as strongly as before. Ironically, Congress's move seems to have given the BJP the political opening it was looking for on this issue. What began as a protest centered on seeking accountability has increasingly been framed as a Congress backed protest versus the BJP. As a result, the focus appears to have shifted from demanding accountability to a broader political confrontation, potentially overshadowing the original concerns that sparked the movement. @Wangchuk66 @GitanjaliAngmo @abhijeet_dipke

As a BJP voter, I have no hesitation in questioning my own govt.
I will ask questions about ethanol blending. I will ask questions about the Ram Mandir donation controversy. I will ask questions about the NEET paper leak. I will demand accountability wherever it is required.

But I also know the difference between seeking accountability and hijacking a genuine issue for political purposes.
The NEET paper leak was a genuine issue. Students deserved justice, accountability, and reforms.
But what started as a students' movement gradually transformed into a much broader political campaign.

Just look at some of the prominent faces associated with the CJP protest:

• Arundhati Roy - Has repeatedly stated that Kashmir was never an integral part of India.

• Colin Gonsalves – Filed a mercy petition on behalf of 26/11 terrorist Ajmal Kasab.

• Prashant Bhushan – Approached the Supreme Court at midnight seeking to stop the execution of terrorist Yakub Memon.

• Kunal Kamra - Insulted Lord Ram and said from the stage, "Yeh log Sita ke Pati ka naam lekar, Nita ke Pati ka kaam kar rahe hain."

• Swara Bhasker – Actress known for supporting the anti-CAA protests, the farmers' protest, and for being a vocal critic of the BJP.

Calls were made from the same platform for the restoration of Article 370.
Demands were also raised for the release of Umar Khalid.
Threats to kill Prime Minister Narendra Modi were also heard from the same protest.

Looking at all this, one simple question arises:
Was this really a movement for NEET students, or had it become a broader anti-BJP political platform?

The violent clashes during the "Chalo Sansad" protest only strengthened that perception. Violence against police personnel, damage to public property, abusive slogans, and dragging unrelated political issues into a students' movement do not help students. They only weaken the credibility of the cause.

I also believe the timing is not a coincidence. Parliament is debating the new FCRA Bill, which seeks to tighten scrutiny of foreign funding. In my view, many organisations and activists who have long benefited from foreign-funded ecosystems see this as a threat, and I believe this protest is connected to it.

The NEET issue is genuine. The demand for accountability is legitimate. But I will not support any attempt to convert a students' movement into a larger political agitation.

And to those outside India who dream of turning India into another Nepal or Bangladesh through instability and street politics-you're mistaken. India is far stronger than you imagine.

Question the govt. Demand accountability. But don't hijack students' future for political agendas.

Peaceful protest ?

Heavy violence broke out last night on Tolstoy Marg in Connaught Place during a protest by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) against the NEET paper leak. Head Constable Babulal and Inspector Nandkishore were attacked with knives and sharp weapons. When ACP Vivek Bhagat rushed forward to rescue them, the mob surrounded him. Protesters used sticks, stones, and sharpened pavement tiles - filed into knife-like points - to assault him. ACP Bhagat was struck on the face, his two teeth were broken; even after he fell, the crowd continued kicking, punching, and hurling abuses at him.

According to the police, some masked goons had infiltrated the protesters. There were clear orders from above not to fire in any situation. The RAF team somehow saved their lives. All this happened in the heart of Delhi - Connaught Place.

CJP, which has turned into an organisation providing protection to criminals in the name of students, repeatedly claims its protests are peaceful. However, repeated targeted attacks on police and anarchy reveal its true character. Such groups are challenging law and order under the guise of a student movement, thereby harming the genuine demands of the youth.

Students returning from the "Chalo Sansad" protest sarcastically applauded Delhi Police and Rapid Action Force personnel as they marched back towards Jantar Mantar after the clashes. Videos from the scene showed protesters clapping and raising slogans following the police action earlier in the day.

Thousands of protesters had gathered in central Delhi as the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) organised the march over alleged NEET paper leaks and examination irregularities. Police stopped the march near Parliament using barricades, tear gas shells and baton charges after protesters attempted to move towards the high security zone.

Delhi Police said around 70 protesters were detained and more than 50 police personnel were injured during the clashes. During the protest, CJP leaders met Union Minister J.P. Nadda and submitted their demands, including the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

Activist Sonam Wangchuk, who is admitted to Safdarjung Hospital, said he would continue his indefinite hunger strike. Opposition leaders criticised the police action and urged the government to engage with the protesting students, while the CJP said the agitation would continue until its demands were addressed.

Chitra Tripathi: छात्रों के प्रदर्शन में गुंडे घुस जाएंगे तो प्रदर्शन का बहुत गलत परिणाम होगा !

आज हमारी Chitra Tripathi जी बहुत दुखी हैं। उनको दुखी देखकर देश का युवा भी दुखी है;

Chitra Tripathi कह रहे हैं, हमने छात्रों की मांग हमेशा ABP News पर उठाई है। सरकार से हमेशा कड़े सवाल पूछे हैं। NEET exam paper leak के खिलाफ हमने सरकार से सवाल पूछा है। हम CJP छात्रों के protest में उनका समर्थन करते हैं।

लेकिन हमारे ABP के साथी reporter को जंतर-मंतर पर reporting करने नहीं दिया गया। उनका camera तोड़ने की कोशिश की गई। बदसलूकी की गई। यह बहुत गलत था। हम हमेशा छात्रों के साथ खड़े होते हैं।

Chitra Tripathi बोलते-बोलते बहुत दुखी नज़र आ रहे हैं।

आप सभी युवाओं से निवेदन है, ABP News की ground reporting पर विरोध मत करिए। उनके सवाल हैं, उसका जवाब अपने तरीके से दीजिए। Chitra Tripathi को भी ground reporting करने का मौका दीजिए। 

"आप लोगों का यही एग्रेसन है की वजह से ग्राउंड रिपोर्टिंग करने नहीं जा रही है आप लोगों का समर्थन करती हैं। सरकार से कड़े सवाल पूछेंगी ,,

किसी भी news channel का camera तोड़ना, mic फेंकना, बदसलूकी करना अच्छी बात नहीं है।

आप student हैं, युवा हैं। आपके पास उनके हर सवाल का जवाब होना चाहिए। जैसे तेवर में जवाब देना है, वैसे दीजिए। कोई रोक नहीं सकता है....

अब कोई आपका पक्ष रखना चाहता है आप किसी को मजबूर कर रहे हैं कि तुम सरकारी न्यूज़ चैनल बनकर ही रहो नेशनल मीडिया नेशनल मीडिया होता है आपकी आवाज़ बहुत दूर तक जाएगी चित्रा त्रिपाठी जी देश का युवा आपका दिल तोड़ने के लिए माफ़ी मांगता है...!

Couldn’t be there physically in Delhi today, but along with millions across the country, my heart and mind were right there on those streets with every single student. 💔
​Today was an intensely emotional, historic day. This march was one of the largest student uprisings in recent memory—a day people will remember for years to come.
​Huge credit to @TheNewspinch for being one of the most dedicated platforms on the ground, capturing every detail—showing how authorities emptied protest sites and blocked entry, only for students to stand united across Central Delhi. 📹
​Seeing the police violence on peaceful youth, Sonam Wangchuk sir has extended his hunger strike (now past Day 23) from hospital detention, demanding accountability.
​To every brave student who faced tear gas, lathi-charges, and police action today: We pray for your speedy recovery and that you get the justice you deserve. You made history today. ✊🇮🇳

CJP started with "Justice for Students."

No political parties. No ideology. Just NEET paper leak and students' future.

Then the narrative changed.

Suddenly, opposition leaders started showing up. Religious remarks sparked outrage. The focus shifted from students to politics.

The students who came in good faith ended up becoming the face of a much larger political battle.

Now it's less about NEET and more about headlines, confrontation, and symbolism.

If your movement begins with students but ends with politicians leading the stage, people have every right to ask:

Was this ever just a students' protest, or was the students' issue the vehicle for something bigger?

Think about it.

Abhijeet Dipke invites the public to join them at Jantar Mantar to continue the agitation against Dharmendra Pradhan. 

The BJP had sent goons to infiltrate the protest and tried to create mischief today. CJP and its protesters have a track record of peaceful protests.

In a significant breakthrough after the protest, CJP representatives Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka met Union Health Minister J.P. Nadda and handed over a written memorandum outlining the group’s key demands. 

The delegation sought the immediate release of Sonam Wangchuk from Safdarjung Hospital, the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, and ₹1 crore compensation for the families of students who allegedly died by suicide over the NEET controversy.

He appealed to the protesters to end their sit-in and cooperate in restoring normalcy, while assuring that the demands would be taken up within the government. body:
Anna Hazare's movement began with one clear demand - Lokpal. The outrage after the Nirbhaya case gave it nationwide momentum, but the sanctity of the stage was never compromised. No politicians were allowed on stage. Anna remained the one and only face of the movement.

CJP on the other hand, began online without any real ground base. Dipke returned to India and launched protests over NEET and education reforms. Then Sonam Wangchuk entered the picture and became the face. But while he was on an indefinite fast, the very same stage saw dance performances and people casually eating in front of him. Later, multiple student organisations and politicians turned that platform into a space for their own agendas...something that should never have been allowed by any sensible person present there.

The moment politics enters a movement, differences of opinion become inevitable. No political protest can command unanimous public support unless it stays anchored to one core demand. Here education reforms gradually took a back seat.

Had they remained uncompromisingly focused on education reforms, the Modi government would eventually have had to respond. But unfortunately, Dipke never looked or acted like a leader. The way he conducted himself throughout the movement made many people stop believing in the very cause they initially supported. And once Sonam Wangchuk was removed from the stage, the rest was only a matter of time #CJPProtest

body:
The government met members of the satirical political group Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) after they held a protest in central Delhi today, sources said. The CJP has been demanding the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the NEET-UG paper leak.

The group's spokesperson @SauravDassss in a post on X said that he and another spokesperson, @AshutoshRanka, met Union minister JP Nadda at his house for 10 minutes.

"While we submit a written letter with our demands, he has assured us that he will meanwhile speak internally. We are in that process..." Das said. More than 50,000 protesters took to the streets of Delhi, demanding accountability over the NEET examination paper leak and broader failures within the education system. Many demonstrators also called for the resignation of the Education Minister and Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

As the crowd marched toward Parliament, Delhi Police and the Rapid Action Force (RAF) reportedly used lathi charges against unarmed protesters. Reports also suggest that hundreds of demonstrators were prevented from joining the march after being blocked inside metro stations.

CJP leader @abhijeet_dipke has reportedly been arrested, while Delhi Police have been accused of assaulting and dragging @Wangchuk66’s wife by her hair.

Meanwhile, much of India’s mainstream media has focused on the government’s narrative, while giving limited attention to the scale, significance, and energy of the demonstrations.

Regardless of political views, the events raise important questions about the right to peaceful protest, accountability, and public trust in institutions. The use of force against demonstrators, the detention of activists, and the marginalization of dissenting voices are developments that deserve careful scrutiny in any democracy.

Amid the controversy, one notable development has been the growing civic engagement of India’s younger generation. Large numbers of Gen Z students, joined by parents who have invested years of hard work and sacrifice in their children’s education, have chosen to speak out and demand transparency, fairness, and meaningful reforms in a system they believe has failed them.

🚨 CJP Founder Abhijeet Dipke Detained During 'Sansad Chalo' Protest

Delhi Police reportedly detained Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke during the party's 'Sansad Chalo' protest demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the alleged NEET-UG paper leak and exam irregularities.

🚔 Initial reports from CJP spokesperson Saurav Das claimed that Dipke had been taken into custody. A short while later, Das clarified that Dipke had not been formally arrested and was safe.

⚠️ As protesters attempted to march towards Parliament by crossing police barricades, security personnel intervened. Police reportedly used lathi-charge and tear gas to disperse the crowd and detained several protesters.

✊ Earlier, Dipke had ended his indefinite hunger strike at Jantar Mantar following an appeal from Ladakh activist Sonam Wangchuk.

🤝 Amid the protests, CJP representatives Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka met Union Health Minister J.P. Nadda to discuss the protesters' demands.

The incident has sparked widespread discussion, with the distinction between detention and formal arrest becoming a key point of debate.

Thousands of people, mostly youths, on Monday took out a protest march in Arunachal Pradesh's capital Itanagar against the alleged wrongful detention of activist Sonam Wangchuk and demanding accountability over alleged examination paper leak scams.

The rally, organised by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), began at Akashdeep and concluded at IG Park, with participants carrying placards, raising slogans and expressing solidarity with Wangchuk, who has been on an indefinite hunger strike for the past two weeks.

The protesters voiced concern over alleged irregularities in competitive examinations, claiming that repeated paper leak incidents had undermined the trust of students and jeopardised the future of lakhs of aspirants.

Wangchuk and the CJP have been campaigning against alleged examination paper leak scams across the country, particularly highlighting the recent NEET paper leak controversy. They have demanded greater accountability in the education system and sought the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

As the procession moved through the city, protesters called for transparency, fairness and integrity in the conduct of examinations, asserting that merit should not be compromised by corruption or malpractice.

Addressing the gathering at IG Park, speakers said the issue affected the future of millions of students and urged the government to introduce comprehensive reforms to restore public confidence in the examination system.

The protest concluded peacefully, with participants reaffirming their support for Wangchuk's agitation and resolving to continue their campaign until concrete measures are taken to strengthen the integrity of India's examination process.

Security forces on Monday used tear gas shells to disperse thousands of supporters of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) who gathered in Delhi to march towards Parliament on the first day of the Monsoon Session, despite police denying permission for the protest.

Police also used sticks and batons to disperse the crowd, comprising mostly youngsters, who had assembled at the Jantar Mantar protest site for the "Chalo Sansad" march. The protesters were demonstrating against alleged irregularities in the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET), the national entrance examination for medical colleges, and demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

According to reports, some protesters and police personnel sustained minor injuries after demonstrators allegedly attempted to breach barricades while marching towards Parliament.

Mobile internet services were also suspended in parts of Central Delhi.

Following the police action, the CJP appealed to its supporters to remain peaceful.

"Even if you've been stopped at certain points, remain calm and maintain peace. We will only win this with peace and love," the party said.

Delhi Police had denied permission for the protest on Sunday and imposed restrictions on large gatherings in the area. Authorities also warned that action could be taken against anyone violating the prohibitory orders.

"Protest marches, processions, demonstrations and assemblies of five or more persons are strictly prohibited, except at the designated protest site at Jantar Mantar, with prior permission," the police said in a post on X.

"Delhi Police appeals to all citizens to respect the law, refrain from participating in any unauthorised gathering or march, and cooperate in maintaining public peace, safety and security," the post read.

A half-hearted, ill-planned, half-baked protest is a disservice to the cause of restoring Kashmir’s dignity and rights.

A party with a Government, 40+ legislators and 5 MPs couldn’t invest the effort to gather 5,000 people in Delhi?

That the CJP protest over NEET has overshadowed the protest by an elected CM, MPs and MLAs is anguishing even for those who stand opposed to the JKNC politically.

What was the need to protest when there was no preparation and no seriousness of intent?

And it is unsurprising that the national opposition leadership seems conspicuously absent. All that warming up to the BJP and humiliating pursuit of a “working relationship” with the BJP has brought this J&K Government to this precarious juncture. And the costs of this ideological isolation and mistrust are to be borne by the people of J&K.

And as for the content and narrative of this “protest”: Not a SINGLE J&K State Flag, not a SINGLE placard mentioning Articles 370 and 35-A OR the cause of Autonomy. What good are the NC resolutions brought and passed in the J&K Assembly (on these issues) with such fanfare and hype when NC itself cannot stand by them in Delhi? Are those resolutions then for local consumption during Assembly and Lok Sabha elections in J&K?

A meek, inert and tamed “demand” for “statehood” in the absence of these political demands is a shameful and undignified constitutional normalization of what was done in 2019. Nothing more, nothing less.

The farmers have protested more seriously. The athletes have protested more seriously. The students have protested more seriously.

Why embarrass the people of J&K by this shoddy excuse of a “protest” which looks more like a NC picnic to Delhi?

Absolutely disheartening and disappointing. And embarrassing.

A people’s uprising in Delhi and all across the country
Lakhs of people have stormed the streets of Delhi and occupied all the roads leading up to the gates of Parliament demanding the immediate resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. For the past month this demand has echoed across the country and various organisations including CJP, AISA organised protests in city after city after 20 lives were lost due to the NEET paper fiasco. The 23 day fast at Jantar Mantar by CJP’s Sonam Wangchuk and AISA’s Neha, Ameen and Manish galvanized the people to take this demand to the logical end calling today’s protest.
The people have answered these calls and gathered in a sea of humanity with the slogans “Inquilab Zindabad”, “Dharmenda Pradan must resign, “Down with the Modi Government”, among others ringing in the air.
This carnival of resistance is the true face of democracy in India. CPIML demands that Dharmenda Pradhan must resign immediately, and the Union Government to steer clear of any crackdown on this festival of democracy. The people are at the gates of Parliament demanding accountability and justice, and that is what they will continue to fight for.

🚨CJP Protest March Live Updates

Tension erupts at Delhi's Jantar Mantar during protest march; police deploy barricades

A large number of protesters, who had gathered at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar on Monday, tried to organise their ‘Chalo Sansad’ march, demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the alleged NEET paper leak issue. The situation turned tense as clashes broke out between police and demonstrators, with security personnel attempting to stop them from crossing barricades. 

The protest witnessed a heavy security presence, with Delhi Police putting up multiple layers of barricading across the New Delhi district to control the movement of protesters. According to police officials, the protesters gathered at the protest site as crowds continued to swell.

Visuals from the spot showed hundreds of students and young protesters carrying flags and raising slogans. Many protesters were seen attempting to move beyond the barricades, following which police personnel repeatedly pushed them back to maintain order.

Police personnel were deployed in large numbers at Jantar Mantar, with a riot control vehicle also entering the protest site early on Monday. Authorities also imposed restrictions around the area as the march towards Parliament was planned by the protesters.

Several students reached Jantar Mantar after gathering near Mandi House Metro Station, raising slogans against the Central government while moving towards the protest venue. The demonstration intensified as more students joined the march.

According to reports from the protest site, police used force to stop demonstrators from crossing security barricades, and a lathi charge was also reported during the confrontation between police and protesters.

The situation remained tense as security personnel attempted to prevent protesters from moving towards restricted areas. The Patel Chowk Metro Station, located near Jantar Mantar, was reportedly closed as a precautionary measure amid the demonstration.

Police also deployed signal jammers in and around the protest area, with some protesters claiming that mobile phone connectivity was affected near the venue.

The protest at Jantar Mantar has been going on for over a month, with its main demand being the resignation of the Union Education Minister over allegations related to the NEET paper leak. The protesters have accused the government of failing to ensure transparency in the examination process and have been demanding accountability from those responsible.

The protest comes amid heightened security arrangements in central Delhi, with police maintaining a strict vigil as demonstrators continue their march and raise slogans over the issue.

》Reports have surfaced about a proposed march to Parliament by CJP tomorrow, July 20.

》Prohibitory orders under Section 163 BNSS (formerly Section 144 CrPC) remain in force across the New Delhi District.

》Parliament session is commencing on July 20.

body:
Exposing the Hijack: Abhijeet Dipke, CJP, and the Alleged Misuse of Sonam Wangchuk at the Jantar Mantar NEET Protest

On 18 July 2026, at Delhi's Jantar Mantar protest site, a woman allegedly threw blue ink at Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP). The incident occurred hours after Delhi Police shifted climate activist Sonam Wangchuk to Safdarjung Hospital following his 20-day hunger strike. Dipke, who had just announced his own indefinite fast, responded on X: "Blue is my colour… Jai Bhim!"

The detained woman later told Aaj Tak and The Tribune that she threw the ink after witnessing what she described as mockery of Lord Shri Ram and Sita Maiya on stage. Calling herself a "staunch Sanatani," she alleged the protest had shifted from demanding NEET reforms to promoting identity politics through repeated "Jai Bhim" slogans. She also claimed CJP was "using Sonam Wangchuk" for political messaging, similar to how Anna Hazare was allegedly used in earlier movements.

The woman further alleged that Dipke's supporters assaulted her before police intervened. These remain her personal claims and have not been independently verified. News reports confirm only that a scuffle occurred after the ink throw and that police detained her.

Separately, Hindu Janajagruti Samiti (HJS) and Supreme Court lawyers also complained about stage content. They objected to remarks by comedian Kunal Kamra concerning Lord Shri Ram and to a performance featuring Faiz Ahmed Faiz's lyrics, alleging both hurt Hindu sentiments. FIRs were demanded against those involved.

Dipke's "Blue is my colour… Jai Bhim!" response reinforced the Ambedkarite symbolism already visible at the protest. While the agitation began over alleged NEET irregularities, critics argue it increasingly blended student issues with ideological messaging. The False Arrest Drama: Abhijeet Dipke’s Manufactured Crisis at Jantar Mantar

In June 2026, Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the provocatively named Cockroach Janata Party (CJP), became the face of a protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over alleged NEET paper leaks, examination irregularities, and student suicides. What began as a time-bound demonstration soon evolved into a narrative centred on alleged state repression.

On 20 June 2026, after Delhi Police denied an extension for the protest, Dipke posted a dramatic video on X (formerly Twitter), declaring:

"Police is about to arrest me. I appeal to you to not stop this peaceful protest nationwide even if I am arrested!"

He urged supporters to launch a "Jail Bharo Andolan" (fill-the-jails movement) across the country while insisting the agitation remain peaceful. The message portrayed the situation as an imminent crackdown on a legitimate student movement.

The reality, however, differed significantly. Delhi Police neither arrested Dipke nor forcibly dispersed the gathering. Despite the protest permission having expired, authorities reportedly allowed protesters to remain at Jantar Mantar overnight. Videos from the site showed police maintaining restraint while demonstrators continued their activities. Within hours, Dipke was reportedly seen eating with supporters, contradicting the impression of an imminent arrest.

The episode exposed what critics describe as a pattern of exaggeration. By predicting his arrest and calling for a nationwide "Jail Bharo Andolan," Dipke attempted to transform the routine enforcement of protest regulations into a national crisis. Such messaging risked portraying law enforcement as aggressors despite the absence of any immediate police action.

Jantar Mantar protests operate under established rules, including time restrictions and prior permission requirements. Extensions are not automatic, and indefinite occupations are generally not permitted. Police allowing the protest to continue overnight despite the expiry of permission reflected restraint rather than repression. Nevertheless, Dipke continued highlighting grievances, including facilities such as water and restrooms, reinforcing a narrative of victimhood.

The strategy appeared aimed at increasing visibility and mobilisation. By presenting himself as a target of state action, Dipke sought to rally students, workers, and farmers under a broader resistance campaign. However, when the predicted arrest never occurred, the dramatic narrative risked undermining the movement's credibility. Genuine concerns over examination integrity became overshadowed by sensational claims.

Critics argue that raising a false alarm of arrest while continuing the protest without detention can delegitimise lawful policing and increase hostility towards officers maintaining public order. Historical examples show that inflammatory rhetoric against police during protests can contribute to unnecessary tensions and violence.

While the concerns surrounding NEET and student welfare deserve serious attention, critics argue that narratives built on exaggerated claims weaken public trust and distract from meaningful reform. In a democracy, the right to protest is fundamental but carries responsibilities, including accurate communication and respect for lawful regulations. Dipke's "Police is about to arrest me" claim, followed by the absence of any arrest and the continuation of the protest overnight, has been cited as an example of political theatre overshadowing verified facts. Genuine reform requires evidence-based advocacy, not manufactured crises that risk turning peaceful demonstrations into flashpoints.

Kapil Sibal’s latest press conference with CJP leaders, pledging ₹1 crore and establishing a nationwide legal aid network for so-called “unjustly targeted” protesters, represents a deeply concerning pattern of selective advocacy that undermines the rule of law in India.

While the right to peaceful protest is fundamental, this initiative appears designed not to protect genuine victims of injustice but to shield those who disrupt public order, spread misinformation, and challenge the democratic mandate of the elected government under the guise of victimhood. 

Senior advocates and public figures like Mr. Sibal have a responsibility to strengthen institutions, not create parallel support systems that encourage frivolous litigation and embolden elements intent on destabilising national progress.

True justice demands accountability for violence, property damage, and attempts to derail critical examinations like NEET that affect millions of aspirants.

By framing legitimate law enforcement actions as persecution, this effort risks eroding public trust in our judiciary and police forces.

India deserves legal professionals who defend the Constitution impartially, not those who consistently align with narratives that weaken the nation’s resolve against internal disruptions.

The people are watching, and such partisan interventions will not go unchallenged in the court of public opinion.

Both India and Italy are being hit by the same playbook right now, violent targeting of Modi, Meloni, and their law enforcement under the cover of “protests.”

In Italy, masked agitators stormed high-speed rail construction sites in Val di Susa. Stones, firecrackers, Molotovs, homemade devices. Over 120 police were hit and injured. Vehicles set ablaze. Organised, premeditated, and far from any spontaneous citizen gathering. Meloni herself called it out as organised violence.

In Delhi, the numbers are almost identical: 118+ police personnel hurt, including senior officers (Special CP, Joint CP, ACPs), during clashes with CJP demonstrators.

Two police buses attacked, shops on Janpath vandalised, stone-pelting, property damage. Police have flagged anti-social elements with criminal records mixing into the crowds via facial recognition. This is definiteluly not a pure “student protest.”

NEET was already reconducted with stricter measures after the paper-leak mess. Stringent action was taken. Yet it was kept alive as a ready-made weapon, exactly the kind of grievance that gets amplified, prolonged, and then turned into street confrontation when the timing suits. We all saw the attacks on police. Uniforms do not make the injuries any less real.

Notice the pattern: simultaneous pressure on the forces that maintain order in two countries whose leaders (Modi and Meloni) have built unusually close personal and strategic ties, Indo-Mediterranean partnership, defence-tech cooperation, open alignment against the usual globalist currents. 

When leaders who refuse the script get stronger, the forces of disruption target the thin blue line that stands between chaos and governance.

This DS has inserted the professional riot cadre, attack the police, flood the narrative with “peaceful students/protesters,” and force governments onto the defensive. Italy’s black-bloc style assault and Delhi’s stone-and-vandalism phase are not coincidence. They are the same method applied on two fronts.

The public should see the method for what it is.

A viral video showing a man in Muslim attire attempting to throw a burning matchstick into the fuel tank of a damaged Mahindra Thar has been falsely shared on social media as footage from the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protest in Delhi, according to an Fact Check investigation.

The video, circulated after the July 20 Parliament march, was shared with claims that it showed a CJP supporter trying to set a vehicle on fire during the protest.

However, Fact Check found that the claim is false. The incident actually took place in Gaya, Bihar, and was unrelated to the NEET protest or the CJP demonstrations.

Using reverse image search, the fact-check team traced the same video to Instagram posts published by CNN-News18 and Moneycontrol on July 18, where it was identified as an incident that occurred following a road accident in Bihar.

According to a Dainik Bhaskar report cited by India Today, a Mahindra Thar collided with a motorcycle and an auto-rickshaw in Gaya, leaving two motorcyclists seriously injured.

Eyewitnesses reportedly claimed that the vehicle bore a BJP sticker and that a woman was driving it, although police did not officially confirm either allegation.

City SDPO Saroj Kumar only confirmed that two persons were injured in the accident and were undergoing treatment.

India Today's local stringer further confirmed that the incident occurred near the Gaya Civil Lines Police Station on July 16.

After the accident, a crowd gathered and some anti-social elements allegedly began pelting stones before attempting to set the vehicle ablaze.

Police later brought the situation under control and registered cases against both the owner and driver of the vehicle, as well as those accused of trying to burn it.

The misleading claim was also amplified by Republic Kannada news anchor Ranjith Shiriyara, who shared the same video multiple times on his social media accounts.

The posts presented the Bihar incident as being connected to the CJP-led NEET protest, despite the video later being fact-checked as unrelated to the Delhi demonstrations.

Meanwhile, the fact-check has gained significance after BJP MLC C.T. Ravi, who recently came under fire for his remarks about "mullahs" during a BJP protest over the NEET controversy in Chikkamagaluru, claimed at a press conference that his comments were made in reference to this viral video.

Ravi had earlier remarked, "What does a mullah have to do with the NEET examination? Even if you tear open his chest, you won't find three letters written there," drawing criticism.

Following a complaint alleging that the speech promoted communal hatred, Chikkamagaluru Town Police registered an FIR against him under provisions relating to promoting enmity and hate speech.

After the FIR was registered, Ravi told reporters that he was referring to the viral video showing a Muslim man trying to set a vehicle on fire and had questioned why such a person would be associated with the NEET protests.

However, the Fact Check establishes that the video Ravi referred to was not from the Delhi protest and had no connection with the CJP agitation.

Instead, it depicted an unrelated incident of mob violence following a traffic accident in Gaya, Bihar. The claim linking the video to the NEET protests was false.

The misleading claim was also amplified by Republic Kannada news anchor Ranjith Shiriyara, who shared the same video multiple times on his social media accounts.

The posts presented the Bihar incident as being connected to the CJP-led NEET protest, despite the video later being fact-checked as unrelated to the Delhi demonstrations.
#FactCheck

🚨STATEMENT

We are deeply concerned by multiple reports reaching us of students and other protestors being targeted, detained, or arrested by various state agencies, particularly in Assam, West Bengal, and Bihar.

The Cockroach Janta Party had called off its nationwide protest only after the Government of India assured us that no punitive action would be taken against any protestor, either now or in the future, in any BJP-ruled or NDA-ruled states. The reports emerging from these states are therefore a matter of grave concern.

First, we wish to assure every protestor that our legal team is already coordinating with brilliant lawyers in the concerned states to secure the release of those detained and to extend all possible legal assistance. This has been happening from Day 1.

Second, we call upon the Government of India, particularly @JPNadda ji and @DrJitendraSingh ji, to immediately honour the assurance given to us by ensuring the release of those detained and by directing that no coercive or retaliatory action is taken against any protestor anywhere in the country. The FIRs registered ought to be withdrawn too.

The Government of India is also reminded of its commitment to furnish us the written guarantee in this regard by tomorrow, Tuesday, 28 July 2026.

Our decision to suspend the nationwide protest was taken in good faith and solely on the basis of the government’s assurance that it would stand by its word. Any departure from that assurance would not merely amount to a breach of trust with the Cockroach Janta Party but would also be a breach of public trust with lakhs of young Indians who chose dialogue over protests.

Such breach of trust will be completely unacceptable to the youth.

The Government of India is reminded that it derives credibility not from just making a promise, but from the promises they honour.

To the young protestors we say, hold on. We are with you. The CJP continues to closely monitor the situation and expects the Government of India and all BJP/NDA state governments to act with utmost urgency, responsibility, and good faith that the present circumstances demand. We demand that all detainees/arrestees be released immediately, and in any case by tomorrow, and that all FIRs be withdrawn immediately, failing which we shall take further necessary steps.

clean_text: 🚨STATEMENT We are deeply concerned by multiple reports reaching us of students and other protestors being targeted, detained, or arrested by various state agencies, particularly in Assam, West Bengal, and Bihar. The Cockroach Janta Party had called off its nationwide protest only after the Government of India assured us that no punitive action would be taken against any protestor, either now or in the future, in any BJP-ruled or NDA-ruled states. The reports emerging from these states are therefore a matter of grave concern. First, we wish to assure every protestor that our legal team is already coordinating with brilliant lawyers in the concerned states to secure the release of those detained and to extend all possible legal assistance. This has been happening from Day 1. Second, we call upon the Government of India, particularly @JPNadda ji and @DrJitendraSingh ji, to immediately honour the assurance given to us by ensuring the release of those detained and by directing that no coercive or retaliatory action is taken against any protestor anywhere in the country. The FIRs registered ought to be withdrawn too. The Government of India is also reminded of its commitment to furnish us the written guarantee in this regard by tomorrow, Tuesday, 28 July 2026. Our decision to suspend the nationwide protest was taken in good faith and solely on the basis of the government’s assurance that it would stand by its word. Any departure from that assurance would not merely amount to a breach of trust with the Cockroach Janta Party but would also be a breach of public trust with lakhs of young Indians who chose dialogue over protests. Such breach of trust will be completely unacceptable to the youth. The Government of India is reminded that it derives credibility not from just making a promise, but from the promises they honour. To the young protestors we say, hold on. We are with you. The CJP continues to closely monitor the situation and expects the Government of India and all BJP/NDA state governments to act with utmost urgency, responsibility, and good faith that the present circumstances demand. We demand that all detainees/arrestees be released immediately, and in any case by tomorrow, and that all FIRs be withdrawn immediately, failing which we shall take further necessary steps. @Cockroachisback

⚠️Trigger Warning: Abusive Language

TG Mohandas, a former head of Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) Intellectual Cell and a political commentator associated with the Rashtiya Swayansevak Sangh (RSS) in Kerala, said the protesters at Jantar Mantar would have been shot and killed if he was in control. He also said the women who were part of the protest like to be raped and would not even complaint if it happens.

The derogatory comments against students and other citizens who participated in the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protest, demanding accountability in the NEET paper leak, in Delhi were made through multiple videos published on a YouTube channel called Pathrika.

In a video published on July 26, he explained how he would handle the situation, if he was in charge. “I will impose a curfew in that area. I will announce the crowd to disperse three times. Then I will shoot, people will scatter and run. Some may die and some may suffer injuries. Within four hours the situation will be calm. The bodies will be collected and taken to hospitals,” he said.

In another video, he said that if the police withdrew from the protest site, rapes would happen.

“Rapes will happen, mass rapes…there are girls who like rape…there are people who like rapes, especially, leftist, secular, democratic, proletarian class of people…if someone dies because of this, they will get a martyr…When mass rapes happen there won't be any complaints, because these are the people who like rape,” Mohandas says in the video.

The videos were published after the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan following a 36-day protest by the CJP.

In another video published on July 24, Mohandas is seen encouraging physical assault on student protesters. He stated that police have every right to hide their name badges and claimed that students were appearing in police uniforms at Jantar Mantar. “Police beat them inside the barricade and outside the barricade; the police were also beaten up,” he said.

Mohandas is a commentator who has a significant following in Kerala. Many have demanded his arrest over the comments.

body:
56 inch Chest with a 26 inch Spine

BJP surrendered to the Cockroach Janata Party. Dharmendra Pradhan resigned. All FIRs against protesters withdrawn. Compensation for NEET victims accepted. Every single demand met. The 37-day protest at Jantar Mantar ended with CJP posting "Cockroaches won. Democracy won."

This did not have to end this way. And one of the main reasons it did is sycophancy.

For those of us who have been following Indian politics long enough, this movie is familiar. We watched it play out with the Congress party over two decades. The script is the same. Only the cast has changed.

Here is how the sycophancy spiral works.

A powerful leader consolidates authority. The people closest to them rise not because of their ability but because of their loyalty. These loyalists tell the leader what the leader wants to hear. Criticism is treated as disloyalty. Disagreement is treated as betrayal. Over time, the leader becomes surrounded by people whose only skill is praise. JP Nadda. Gogoi. Sanjay Jha. Digvijay Singh. Different parties, same species. They thrive not by being strong but by making the leader feel strong.

The problem is not that these people are sycophants. The problem is what sycophancy does to the information flow.

BJP's own supporters have been demanding Pradhan's resignation for months over the NEET examination scandal. Students died by suicide. Parents were devastated. The anger was real, widespread, and legitimate. But the people around Modi told him it was a non-issue. That the noise would die down. That the party's core support would hold. That Pradhan need not resign because resigning would show weakness.

This is what sycophants do. They filter reality. They present the world as the leader wants to see it, not as it is. And the leader, addicted to the dopamine of constant positive feedback, treats any dissonance as noise rather than signal. When you are in a sycophantic spiral, you are so accustomed to praise that even mild criticism feels like an attack. So you default to more praise. More reassurance. More "everything is fine, sir."

Until it is not fine. Until a satirical movement born from a Chief Justice's insult to unemployed youth puts people on the street and forces your Health Minister to sit across from two 20-somethings and accept every demand they put on the table.

Watch the footage of Nadda meeting the CJP representatives. This is India's Health Minister, a senior BJP leader, practically begging for a handshake. This is what sycophancy produces. Not strength. Weakness dressed in a party robes. When the moment demanded firmness, strategic communication, and a genuine engagement with legitimate grievances, the party sent a man whose instinct was to surrender because he had never been trained to fight. He was trained to agree.

Nadda showed BJP's core voters that the 56-inch chest has deputies with 26-inch spines.

This is the real cost. Elections are not won by core voters alone. Core voters will vote BJP no matter what. But elections are won by swing voters. And swing voters are watching. They are watching Nadda fumble. They are watching the party that projects strength act from weakness. They are watching a satirical Instagram movement outmaneuver the most formidable political machine in Indian history.

Even if swing voters are lost, core voters can be demoralized. They may never switch loyalties. But they may not show up at the polling booth. The dissonance for them is real. They signed up for a party that fights. A party that does not bend. When they see their leaders bend on national television, the gap between the party's self-image and its behavior becomes too wide to ignore. They may not articulate it. But the enthusiasm fades. The booth-level energy drops. The margins shrink.

Congress walked this exact path. A formidable force reduced to losing official opposition status within a decade. Not because the public turned against them overnight. But because the sycophants drowned out the grassroots leaders. Because the Digvijay Singhs, Gogois, Mani Shankars and Sanjay Jhas rose while the genuine talent was sidelined. Because the leadership stopped hearing the truth and started hearing only what made them comfortable.

BJP has one structural advantage Congress never had: it is not wedded to a dynasty. It has the RSS's organizational depth. It has a self-correction mechanism. But sycophancy corrodes self-correction. When the leadership structure is infested with weak men who have no real connect or command, the mechanism rusts.

Modi and Shah can clean house. They can replace the Naddas with fighters. They can rebuild the feedback loops that once made BJP the most responsive political organization in the country. But that requires acknowledging that the problem exists. And acknowledging that the problem exists requires hearing it from someone other than a sycophant.

That is the trap. And it is the same trap Congress walked into. And in all likelihood, BJP will continue to walk into.

body:
Before BJP IT Cell floods your feed with...
"Modi Masterstroke."
Let's call it what it looks like.
A "Stupidstroke."

Dharmendra Pradhan had to go.
No debate.

India's education system is rotten.
It needed surgery.

Not slogans.
Not committees.
Not another press conference.

A complete overhaul.

But timing is everything.

The government did not remove him after reform.
It removed him after pressure.

And that changes everything.

CJP had no proven national student base.
No moral legitimacy to dictate terms to the Government.

Yet this government served legitimacy to it...
On a silver platter.

Now they can proudly say:
"We forced a Union Minister to resign."

Congratulations!!!

You have just manufactured a political brand.

Tomorrow...
A political party.
A pressure cartel.
An unelected veto machine.

A B-team of AAP that quietly slices BJP's own vote bank.

BJP has seen this movie before.

It surrendered the Farm Laws.
Now it has surrendered a Minister.

Not because accountability was wrong.

But because the street learnt something far more dangerous.

Pressure works.
Or worse...
Violence works.

That is the real headline.

Once a protest tastes blood...
It doesn't ask for dessert.
It asks for the kitchen.

Today...
Dharmendra Pradhan.

Tomorrow...
Action against the police.

Then another Minister.
Then the Home Minister.

Eventually...
Narendra Modi.

What a Masterstroke.

Bravo.

You didn't end the protest.
You upgraded its business model.

When governments reward pressure...
Pressure becomes policy.

When governments reward street muscle...
Street muscle becomes strategy.

And when survival becomes more important than reform...
Reform is the first casualty.

The tragedy is this.

Nobody will now discuss NEET reforms.
Nobody will discuss NTA reforms.
Nobody will discuss paper leaks.
Nobody will discuss fixing the system.

The system disappears.
The spectacle survives.

CJP has not ended.
It has just learnt one lesson.

The Government can be made to kneel.

Dear @narendramodi @PMOIndia @dpradhanbjp @JoshiPralhad 🙏

Just heard an interesting conversation near the lift lobby of my apartment.

A few girls were talking about the NEET protest. One of them said, "Look at the NEET protest by CJP. They got justice by forcing the Education Minister to resign." Another added, "The Education Minister doesn't even know how to write a resignation letter."

One of the girls recognised me and said, "Sorry, uncle. We didn't mean anything bad." Then she asked, "Uncle, what do you think?"

By then, the lift had arrived and we all got in.

I just told her, "Never believe the first piece of information you receive on any app. Verify it. Read more. Dig deeper. See who is saying it, what their background is, and what kind of language they themselves have used in public. After that, form your own opinion. The decision is yours."

My floor arrived, and I stepped out.

That conversation stayed with me.

We can criticise people we disagree with, and everyone has the right to question public figures. But what worries me more is how quickly misinformation and propaganda spread through social media. Many young people end up believing the first version of a story they see without checking if it is even true.

At that age, it is easy to believe that every movement is a revolution and that every resignation is the solution to a problem. Real life is much more complicated than that.

The bigger concern is that we are slowly losing our children to misinformation. They deserve facts, not manipulation.

So instead of ignoring them or shouting at them, let us talk to them. Encourage them to question, verify, and think for themselves.

That is our responsibility as parents, elders, teachers, and as a society.

▪️Senior Advocate Kapil Sibal joined the CJP press conference and announced a contribution of ₹1 crore towards legal assistance for students facing cases.
▪️CJP will launch a dedicated website to connect students booked in protest-related cases with lawyers across the country on a district-wise basis.

▪️CJP appealed to lawyers nationwide to join the legal initiative, saying it would encourage affected students.
▪️Saurav Das said CJP had resolved after July 20 to take legal action against police personnel allegedly responsible for "unjustified" lathi-charge on protesters.
▪️CJP said the government had agreed that FIRs registered against protesters would be withdrawn, and that a written copy of the agreement would be provided on Tuesday.
▪️The organisation expressed hope that no protesters would be harassed. However, it warned that if detained protesters are not released, CJP would be compelled to resume its protests.

Q)Why accountability asked only to BJP centre not state Govts ?
CJP said NEET paper leak was the trigger point for the nationwide movement and reiterated that everyone responsible for paper leaks must be held accountable, adding that the same standard of accountability should apply to all future cases in other states as well.

18-year-old NEET aspirant Sharim allegedly died by suicide on 13 June following the alleged NEET-UG paper leak controversy. A resident of Amarpur village in Uttar Pradesh's Bulandshahr district, Sharim had been preparing for NEET at Aakash Institute in Jasola, Delhi.

His elder brother, Firoz Qureshi, says he has been seeking justice ever since. According to Firoz, he first approached the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), requesting that Sharim's photograph and details be displayed on the protest stage, but alleges that his request was ignored.

Firoz further claims that on 15 June, he went to Shaheen Bagh Police Station to file a complaint, but alleges that the police did not take his concerns seriously.

According to Firoz, he made one final attempt on the last morning of the Jantar Mantar protest to raise his brother's case with CJP representatives, but says he was once again ignored.

STORY | Anti paper leak bill with stricter punishment introduced in Lok Sabha

Government on Monday introduced a bill in the Lok Sabha to amend the anti-paper leaks law with stricter punishment of up to 10 years in jail and a Rs 50 lakh fine, within days of large-scale student protests against the NEET fiasco rocking the nation that forced Dharmendra Pradhan to resign as education minister.

The proposed legislation was introduced by Minister of State for PMO Jitendra Singh amidst protests and sloganeering by the Opposition demanding a response from the government over the police crackdown on students during the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)-led July 20 protest march to Parliament.

According to the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026, investigations into paper leak cases are to be completed within two months.

The bill says that individuals involved in paper leaks or unfair means in exams will get jail terms for a minimum of 5 years and a maximum of 10 years and a fine of up to Rs 50 lakh.

For organised crimes, the bill proposes a minimum sentence of seven years and a fine of up to Rs 10 crore.

A Conversation That Confirmed What I Was Already Thinking.

This morning, my phone rang. The caller is a hardcore NCP, Congress, and Shiv Sena (UBT) sympathiser who also holds an important organisational position in one of the MVA parties.

After the usual greetings, our conversation naturally shifted to the ongoing NEET protests—the aftermath, why they happened, and what they could mean for the BJP now.

Let me make one thing clear: he is an MVA sympathiser. Yet what he said echoed almost exactly what had been running through my own mind.

Last week, I had written that the BJP's political calculations had gone badly wrong in the NEET paper leak issue. The matter escalated to the point where the Prime Minister had to release three videos, a Union Minister resigned, and the government found itself on the defensive.

First, the BJP has historically been quick to recognise public sentiment and respond when the mood on the streets becomes impossible to ignore. That does not mean it will now bow to every protest. If anything, this episode should encourage the government to become more transparent, accountable, and proactive. Secondly, So those of you, expecting now protests will be the next big thing all the time, dream on!

The next issue brewing up is the ethanol controversy 

Tehseen Poonawalla has raised questions that deserve answers, and it increasingly appears that Nitin Gadkari could become the next political target. Unlike former Union Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, Gadkari has had a much longer public and political career, giving opponents far more material to scrutinise. Whether that translates into anything substantial remains to be seen.

Coming back to my conversation, the MVA sympathiser told me something I completely agreed with.

He said:

"Vikrant, even many people on the Right did not like what happened during these protests. Even many of the Right too supported the students and demanded transparency, but the abusive attacks on the Prime Minister, the assault on policemen, and the destruction of public property crossed the line."

I agreed.

The genuine students who sparked this movement should never become collateral damage. If peaceful students have faced punitive action, the government should review those cases and withdraw action wherever appropriate.

Interestingly, CJP founder Dipke himself acknowledged that anti-India elements and disruptive groups had infiltrated the protests to hijack a legitimate student movement.

What Exactly Is CJP's Objection?

Dipke had earlier stated that those responsible for violence, abusive slogans, and unlawful acts were outsiders who did not represent his supporters.

If that is indeed the case, then shouldn't CJP support action against those specific individuals instead of opposing the entire law enforcement process?

Those who attacked police personnel, vandalised public property, or attempted to derail a peaceful student movement should face the law. Innocent students, however, should be protected.

If CJP itself accepts that anti-social elements infiltrated the protests, then why is it now objecting to the government's action against those accused of violence?

That is a question that deserves an answer.

A New Lease of Life for the Opposition in Maharashtra? 

There is little doubt that this episode has injected fresh energy into an opposition that had appeared politically dormant, particularly in Maharashtra. Dipke has, for the moment, given it a rallying point.

However, Maharashtra is a politically unique state.

Many opposition parties may now attempt to replicate this strategy through younger leaders such as Aaditya Thackeray and Rohit Pawar. But there is one major difference.

People are still trying to understand who Dipke is. Leaders such as Aaditya Thackeray, Rohit Pawar, Uddhav Thackeray, and Raj Thackeray are already familiar political faces. Voters have watched them for years and have largely formed their opinions.

For that reason, I am not convinced that the same political formula will produce identical results in Maharashtra.

Even if much of Bollywood or other influential voices oppose the BJP, Maharashtra's politics has traditionally been shaped more by local political realities than celebrity endorsements.

Whether this momentum becomes a lasting political movement or remains a temporary surge of public anger is something only time will answer.

Vikrant Meena Hemant Joshi.

Mumbai-based model Rhiya Ahir, who went viral after standing in front of a police van carrying detained protesters during the CJP's agitation over the alleged NEET paper leak, has filed a police complaint alleging a coordinated online hate campaign against her. The 27-year-old claimed old photographs and social media posts from her modelling career were edited and circulated to slut-shame her and target her family. She said police have contacted her following the complaint, and she is expected to meet Maharashtra Cyber Cell authorities to pursue the matter further.

Rhiya had become one of the most recognisable faces of the protest after a video showed her standing in front of a police van at Mumbai's Shivaji Park, demanding the release of detained protesters. She said she acted spontaneously after seeing people being taken away, adding that she did not personally know those inside the vehicle. She also alleged that the driver repeatedly revved the engine in an attempt to intimidate her, but she refused to move.

🚩I was part of the protest march in Delhi, saw democratic politics take a new turn

(Sensible Article by  YOGENDRA YADAV,who says Parliament and much of Lutyens' Delhi was packed with the protesters. It was India's "Oc-cupy moment. Anger against Minister Dharmendra Pradhan is only the tip of the iceberg. The underlying urge is for an equitable, meaningful and quality education and for a universal right to employment.For many months now, I have been re-peating a dialogue to anyone who asks me about the future of India: "Sawal ye nahin hai kijanatatanashahi ke khilaaf kharihogi ya nahin. Sawal sirf itna hai ki jab janata kharihogitab tak kahin ham toh nahin baith jayenge". Yesterday, I saw it unfold before my eyes )

THE REGIME-and the silence - often made me wonder whether I'm completely crazy for coming back... But today  to see this democratic spirit which has been silenced for so long come back alive again - I feel whole again. Even if temporarily".

I read these lines well past 3 am, still trying to process all that I had witnessed on the streets of Delhi this Monday. These lines, posted on X by Vanya Vaidehi Bhargav, her-self a fine political theorist, captured why July 20 may be remembered in the history of Indian democracy.

This column has argued that as we slip from competitive authoritarianism to electoral autocracy, the focus of the Opposition must switch from electoral politics to a politics of resistance. Here are six reasons why the Jantar Mantar protest was a perfect illustration of what the politics of resistance may look like.

Firstly, the numbers. No one has a good estimate. But it was undoubtedly many times more than the 15,000-20,000 the or ganisers had hoped and planned for. Drone images suggest that well over a lakh joined this protest. Originally planned as a march, it turned into a rally, then a raila a mass flow. By the afternoon, every road leading to

Parliament and much of Lutyens' Delhi was packed with the protesters. It was India's "Oc-cupy moment.

What made the numbers stand out even more is that this was an organic mobilisation. Far from the culture of rent-a-crowd political rallies or spectacles of organisa-tional prowess, the Jantar Mantar protest comprised almost entirely self-mobilised youth responding to a social media call, ar-anging for their travel and walking long distances. The last time I witnessed this spontaneous synchronisation was the fa-mous Republic Day tractor march organ-ised by the farmers' movement in 2021.

Third, notice their "utterly absurd diversity", as a friend called it. I met a person who travelled from Arunachal Pradesh, a group of adults from Dharamshala in Himachal Pradesh, a wheel-chair bound student of Spanish, a group of girls from Dehradun, scores of boys and girls from all over UP, Bihar and MP, students from elite private universities, national public universities as well as time-pass colleges, and of course a large chunk of "aspirants" from Mukherjee Nagar and similar hotspots. The proportion of women was striking and exhilarating. These were not your usual suspects. An overwhelming majority were first-time par-ticipants in any protest. Their families mostly supported the BJP. So did they, till yesterday. That must worry the regime.

Fourth, the issue that brought them together was much larger and more enduring than just the recent paper leaks. There were, of course, students who suffered the NEET cancellation and the CBSE scam, parents who lost their children due to this fiasco, aspirants waiting indefinitely for jobs, and victims of recruitment scams. But more than direct sufferers, the protesters were primarily potential sufferers, those who know that it could be their turnto-morrow, those who realise that the educa-tion-employment system has broken down.

More than direct sufferers , the protesters were primarily potential sufferers, those who know that it could be their turn tomorrow, those who realise that the education-employment system has broken down

Anger against Minister Dharmendra Pradhan is only the tip of the iceberg. The underlying urge is for an equitable, meaningful and quality education and for a universal right to employment. It is after half a century-since the JP movement in Bihar in 1974-that a youth protest has placed education and employment at the centre of the national agenda.

Fifth, the spirit of resistance goes beyond names and labels. Sonam Wangchuk is clearly their hero, but the hero-worship quo-tient is much more muted than during the Anna movement. The youth related to the CJP and its leadership, but were not shy to offer healthy criticism. They heard and cheered political leaders and activists from the podium, but were not swayed by anyone personality. This democratic spirit augurs well for the future.

Sixth, the repeated chants of "Godi media, go back" were a reminder that the youth have found a way past the narratives of mainstream media. For the last one

month, the Noida channels and the notional press more or less erased the protest at Jantar Mantar, when not mocking or demonising it. Yet every calculation of the regime and every narrative of its spin doctors was defied. Just as in the farmers' movement, media black-outs ac tually spurred the participants into developing their parallel informa-tion channels through social media, word of mouth and Whats-

App. Their posters were punchy: "The true test of a democracy isn't the protest. It'show the state responds to it". Their slogans were innovative. I heard this one for the first time: "Jab jab Modi darta hai, Hindu-Muslim karta hai". The authoritarian narrative is being punctured.

Seventh, and above all, July 20 shows a fracturing of the spell of fear. Today's youth understand the risks of surveillance and pro-filing under the present regime, something absent during the Ramlila Maidan mobilisa-tion of the anti-corruption movement. That deterred many of them from coming to Jan-tar Mantar for the first two weeks. But somehow, something shattered it on Monday. Perhaps the safety of the crowd. Perhaps the adrenaline of hopelessness. Or maybe a faint hope. But these young people were not afraid of being heard, photo-graphed or even tear-gassed.

Finally, in a way almost unnoticed, the movement could mark a new phase in the politics of social justice. The youth of India have come together in a movement led by a Dalit, Abhijeet Dipke, and inspired by an Adi-vasi, Sonam Wangchuk, one not limited to the stereotypical "SC/ST issues". Instead of demanding its share in the nation, bahujan politics can now define what the nation is.

For many months now, I have been re-peating a dialogue to anyone who asks me about the future of India: "Sawal ye nahin hai kijanatatanashahi ke khilaaf kharihogi ya nahin. Sawal sirf itna hai ki jab janata kharihogitab tak kahin ham toh nahin baith jayenge". Yesterday, I saw it unfold before my eyes. 

The writer is member, Swaraj India, and national convenor, Bharat Jodo Abhiyaan. Views are personal
