🚩Modi govt can’t see the difference between confidence and arrogance. What it means to people ?

(It’s not just about the NEET paper leaks anymore. It’s not even about Dharmendra Pradhan. The huge gathering is a cumulative effect of small grievances that have been building up.When protesters talk about the government’s refusal to engage with the youth, they are only voicing their frustration with a system in which they have no say.)

In the 2016 film Sultan, Anushka Sharma’s character gives her wrestler-husband Sultan—played by Salman Khan—a stinging rebuke for ‘earning’ arrogance while she wanted him to earn respect: “Maine tujhe izzat kamaane ko kaha tha. Tu toh guroor kamaa ke aa gaya Sultan.” Many Indians may relate to her better now.

On Monday, the might of the State was on display as the police lathicharged and used tear gas to prevent thousands of young demonstrators from reaching the Parliament to protest against irregularities in medical entrance examinations and demand the resignation of Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Activist Sonam Wangchuk, who was on fast for three weeks before being forcibly taken to Safdarjung Hospital, couldn’t join them as he said he was under ‘illegal detention’.

Even as thousands of students were struggling to cross police barricades to reach the Parliament, Prime Minister Narendra Modi delivered his customary address before the start of the session. He made no mention of what was happening to India’s youth barely a few hundred metres from where he stood. As if they didn’t matter! Lauding the successful launch of a rocket by a Hyderabad-based company, he took a not-so-veiled swipe at Rahul Gandhi, saying that the feat was achieved by those with an average age of 28 years, “not some 56-year-old young man”. It was out of context. The joke was supposed to be on the 56-year-old Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha. But its timing—with the State’s brute power on display against students and youth in the national capital—seemed to be a reminder of the 56-inch chest, a metaphor for a strong and decisive government.

Manmohan Singh’s ‘mistake’?

Let me first play the devil’s advocate. Aspiring doctors, students, and youth in general need to understand that PM Modi doesn’t speak on anything that is negative about his government. He doesn’t want to repeat the mistakes made by former Prime Minister Manmohan Singh and then-UPA chairperson Sonia Gandhi, who easily buckled under the Opposition’s pressure and yielded to public outrage. Remember how many Union ministers and chief ministers they sacrificed: external affairs minister Natwar Singh over Oil-For-Food scandal; Union home minister Shivraj Patil for 26/11 terror attack—actually for changing his clothes way too often during that crisis; Maharashtra CM Vilasrao Deshmukh for its inept handling—actually for giving a tour of terror-hit Taj to his actor son Riteish and filmmaker Ram Gopal Varma; Deshmukh’s successor Ashok Chavan for the Adarsh scam; Union law minister Ashwani Kumar for alleged interference in a Central Bureau of Investigation probe; and many more.

A senior Congress leader once told me about his conversation with Sonia Gandhi, who apparently conceded to him that asking the Union ministers and CMs to resign was a mistake, as it only made the Opposition more strident. I wouldn’t call it a mistake, though. A democratically elected government must respond to public sentiments even if it has to pay a political cost. The Modi government obviously doesn’t see it this way.

Lakhs of students and their families may be feeling outraged over the NEET-UG paper leak and lapses and irregularities in other examinations. The Modi government won’t, however, yield to their demand for the education minister’s resignation, as it would be a sign of weakness. How did the show of respect for public sentiment serve the Manmohan Singh government? It only made people more demanding and unforgiving, making the UPA government look increasingly weak. The UPA government folded under public support for Anna Hazare’s fast-unto-death within 12 days and yielded to his demand. This laid the foundation for the UPA’s eventual ouster. Do you even remember if the Lokpal exists today?

Anyway, this should explain the Modi government’s refusal to even acknowledge the protests by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and Wangchuk’s three-week-long fast. When it threatened to become a ‘nuisance’ in front of Parliament, the police just bundled Wangchuk out to a hospital. His wife wants to shift him to a private facility, but the authorities won’t let her do that.

The government was obviously taken aback on Monday. It probably didn’t expect students and youth from across the country to move beyond social media and descend on the country’s capital in thousands in support of Wangchuk and the CJP. Health minister JP Nadda had to give an audience to a CJP delegation as the police lathicharged and tear gas didn’t seem to break the morale of young protesters. The only other time the Modi government buckled in the past was when it had to scrap the farm laws due to farmers’ prolonged protests on Delhi’s borders. I am not sure yet if the government finds Monday’s protest electorally alarming enough to make a second exception.

The Modi government needs to do a rethink. Listen to what these young protesters are saying. It’s not just about the NEET paper leak anymore. It’s not even about Dharmendra Pradhan. Among the protesters were teenagers who have passed out of prestigious public schools in the national capital and even got admission in Delhi University. They weren’t affected by the paper leak, but they were coming to Jantar Mantar to do what many of them said was their ‘moral duty’. The government’s refusal to even engage with protesting students and Wangchuk is precisely what has triggered these teenagers and youth. Members of students’ organisations affiliated to some political parties did lend support, and some parties did bring in their supporters, but it would be a mistake for the government to look at the crowds on Delhi roads as the work of the political Opposition.

Bubbling beneath the surface

The NEET paper leak is just the latest trigger. The huge gathering seems to be a cumulative effect of small grievances that have been building up. When protesters talk about the government’s refusal to engage with the youth, they are only voicing their frustration with a system in which they have no say.

Take, for instance, the government’s diktat about the three-language policy in CBSE schools, which stipulates two native Indian languages, with English virtually becoming a foreign language. I have met so many students and parents, including many Modi supporters, who are upset with this imposition. They see it as a virtual imposition of Sanskrit and an exclusion of foreign languages. Say, if a child is studying in a Delhi school, they would opt for Hindi as one of the native languages and English as the third language. As for the second native language, the choice is severely limited. Students may want to opt for Kannada, Tamil, Telugu, Bengali, Gujarati, or Marathi as the second native language. A school would find it difficult to hire teachers for each of these languages. It’s easier to hire a Sanskrit teacher to meet the second native language criterion. And what if students—and their parents—want a foreign language to be taught in the school? They can’t, because the government won’t let them.

Did the government ask these parents and students what they wanted? No. If someone aspires to become a doctor and join King George’s Medical University in Lucknow, they must become a vegetarian first. Because UP governor Anandiben Patel is a vegetarian. While the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leaders went on a non-veg binge before the West Bengal Assembly elections, one of the first things the party did after coming to power was to exclude eggs from mid-day meals in schools. Were the parents consulted? No. One BJP-ruled state after another has been bringing laws to regulate live-in relationships, prescribing fines and imprisonment for not registering. Were the youth—or their parents—asked if they would like the government to pry into their bedrooms? No. People have other grouses, too. To cite just one instance, they don’t know what to do with their cars as the government’s sudden decision to increase ethanol blending to 20 per cent has reduced the vehicles’ mileage and could potentially damage them.

These are just a few of many, many grievances the youth have. They hear just one response from the government: “I am your benefactor. I give your parents free foodgrains, free medical facilities, cash, and what not. Don’t ask questions. We know what’s good for you. Ask not what the government should do for you, but what you can do for us.”

PM Modi may want to rethink such messaging.

DK Singh is Political Editor at ThePrint. H

While the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leaders went on a non-veg binge before the West Bengal Assembly elections, one of the first things the party did after coming to power was to exclude eggs from mid-day meals in schools. Were the parents consulted? No. One BJP-ruled state after another has been bringing laws to regulate live-in relationships, prescribing fines and imprisonment for not registering. Were the youth—or their parents—asked if they would like the government to pry into their bedrooms? No. People have other grouses, too. To cite just one instance, they don’t know what to do with their cars as the government’s sudden decision to increase ethanol blending to 20 per cent has reduced the vehicles’ mileage and could potentially damage them. These are just a few of many, many grievances the youth have. They hear just one response from the government: “I am your benefactor. I give your parents free foodgrains, free medical facilities, cash, and what not. Don’t ask questions. We know what’s good for you. Ask not what the government should do for you, but what you can do for us.” PM Modi may want to rethink such messaging. DK Singh is Political Editor at ThePrint. H

body:
Mission Accomplished… Protest Called Off! 🎭
Finally, the agitation at Jantar Mantar has come to an end and the protests are called off.
If you watched the evening TV news discussions, the faces of the opposition spokespersons said it all. They looked so disappointed! It almost felt like they were unhappy that the issue got resolved peacefully without creating more chaos. 

For weeks, political parties and groups like CJP were shouting on the streets. 

But let us ask one simple, honest question: Did CJP or any opposition leader give even ONE good, practical suggestion on how to reform NEET or improve the exam system?
The answer is a big NO. 
Zero suggestions
zero plans
zero interest in the real future of the students. 
It was all just political drama to target the Modi government.

While they were busy making noise, look at what the Central Government is actually doing on the ground to protect our students:
 Moving towards Computer-Based Testing (CBT) wherever possible, so physical paper leaks during printing and transport are stopped completely.
 Question papers will be sent directly to exam centers through encrypted digital vaults.
 Using Aadhaar-based biometric verification at centers so no fake candidate or impersonator can enter.
 Deploying Artificial Intelligence (AI) to catch suspicious activities and tampered OMR sheets.
 Strengthening cybersecurity with special IT agencies and forming a National Technical Committee to set strict protocols for all competitive exams.
 Enforcing the strict Public Examinations Act 2024, which brings severe punishments—up to 10 years in jail and a ₹10 crore fine for paper leak mafias.
This is the real difference. One side used students for political gain and television attention. The Modi Government, on the other hand, worked silently to bring real, permanent solutions for our youth.
Our students deserve a clean system, not political games! 🤝🇮🇳
— Shone George

The more you analyse why we see so many videos which are abusing the PM especially done by girls the more you realise the protests in the age of Internet are not just protests but a viral moment.

The moment the agitation became viral, it stopped being about NEET and turned into something else entirely. 

In the attention economy, once a cause starts generating high engagement, it acquires a life of its own. For a generation that lives inside social media, visibility itself becomes the reward.

Gen Z does not just use platforms. There lives are on them. Status, identity, and self-worth are increasingly measured in reach, shares, and perceived moral positioning. 

When a protest offers the chance to be seen as righteous, brave, and relevant, the dopamine hit is powerful. 

Each viral video, each round of applause from the online crowd reinforces the behaviour. The cause becomes secondary to the feeling of mattering.

There is also a deeper psychological layer. Young people are naturally more idealistic. They have a stronger need for moral clarity and a lower tolerance for perceived injustice. 

When this idealism collides with the attention economy, protests become very strong. Participating feels both virtuous and rewarding. It satisfies the desire to do something meaningful while simultaneously delivering social validation.

This combination is why the CJP protests gained traction so quickly and proved difficult to contain. It was not just organisational strength or political backing. 

It was the fusion of idealism with a dopamine driven attention system that constantly rewarded escalation and visibility.

This is the new terrain. Protests that successfully plug into the attention economy do not follow the old rules.

India’s Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan Resigns Amid Student Protests

India’s Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan has announced his resignation amid prolonged student protests and political pressure. In a letter posted on the social media platform X (formerly Twitter) on Saturday (July 25), he announced his resignation.
According to various Indian media reports, Dharmendra Pradhan has already submitted his resignation to Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Hours after the resignation announcement, a third round of talks was scheduled to take place between the protesting organization Kokroch Janata Party (CJP) and representatives of the central government.

The protesters, who had been staging a sit-in at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar for more than a month, had three major demands. Their primary demand was the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. They also demanded assurances that no legal action would be taken against participating students and compensation of INR 10 million for the families of students who died by suicide following the alleged NEET question paper leak.

Two rounds of talks had previously been held between the government and the protesters, but no agreement was reached over the education minister’s resignation. On Saturday morning, the CJP made it clear that it would not engage in further talks with the government unless Dharmendra Pradhan was removed or resigned.

Against this backdrop, Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation is being viewed as a significant development in the ongoing protest movement.

body:
What did the protest at Jantar Mantar achieve ?
By Justice Katju
The Cockroach Janta Party ( CJP ) protest which began on 19th June 2026 at Jantar Mantar, Delhi, ended on 25th July with the resignation of the Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan and acceptance of 2 other demands of the CJP by the government, with great celebration and revelry by the protestors.
What has it achieved ? Nothing, and yet something. Let me explain.
The entire agitation was focused on the demand for resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan. Why ? Because of paper leaks in the NEET examinations
https://t.co/UJD0mRsP3U
But why are there paper leaks ? Because of corruption. Corruption is rampant in India, in almost every sphere, not just in NEET.
So paper leaks will continue as long as corruption continues in India. And corruption will continue in India, as the Anna Hazare anti-corruption movement of 2011 has proved. The movement started with great fanfare, and soon acquired a huge following in India, but later on fizzled out, with nothing achieved. In fact many believe that corruption is even more today, and at every level.
So resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan has only resulted in his replacement by another Education Minister, but it will have no effect in paper leaks, since corruption will continue in India.
So has the CJP protest achieved nothing ? I believe it has achieved something important.
Till now there were 2 narratives prevailing in India.
The first was that India was progressing, with the fastest growing economy in the world and rise in GDP, and had already surpassed Japan and would soon surpass Germany, making the Indian economy the third largest in the world.
https://t.co/NZQTQoWBEm
https://t.co/JVOM8nNhZI
The second was that in fact the Indian economy was stagnant ( if not in recession ), with record and rising unemployment, skyrocketing prices of food and other essential commodities, appalling level of child malnutrition ( every second Indian child is malnourished, according to Global Hunger Index ), almost total lack of proper healthcare and good education for the masses, etc.
https://t.co/xoX5Ugsmve
https://t.co/UMcYHolCE0
https://t.co/jDTWBbOAVz
https://t.co/QtrHWCj9JY
https://t.co/xfso7t7AXZ
https://t.co/PgTKASTMZJ
Many people were confused as to which narrative was correct.
The CJP movement has in a flash removed the confusion, and proved that the second narrative is correct. This became evident when within a few days of creation ( as a satire ) of the CJP its creator Abhijeet Dipke, a student of Boston University, got over 20 million followers
https://t.co/UJD0mRsP3U
The cause of this huge response to the CJP is the massive unemployment in India, which has reached a record level.
12 million youth are entering the job market in India every year, but less than half a million jobs are created annually in the organized sector of the Indian economy. So where do the remaining 11.5 million go ? They become hawkers, street vendors, bouncers, stringers, criminals, beggars, or end up as suicides, and many girls become prostitutes. If a single peon's ( chaprasi ) job is advertised by the government there are usually thousands of applicants, some even with Ph.D. MBA, https://t.co/p6awnfZTgl, or engineering degrees.
The looming spectre of unemployment after they complete their education is in the minds of most Indian youth. This is the real cause of the huge numbers of supporters which the CJP movement has acquired so quickly.
But it is only an emotional response, and will not solve the unemployment problem, nor of paper leaks.
The government has announced that it is bringing a Bill in Parliament for imposing a sentence of upto 10 years imprisonment for those involved in paper leaks.
To my mind this will only give another handle to the police to extort money, as experience has shown.
Moreover, even if paper leaks are checked, it will only mean that meritorious students will get admission instead of non meritorious ones. But it will not increase the number of available jobs in the country.
Jobs can be increased and unemployment largely abolished when the economy is rapidly expanding. But this rapid expansion of the economy is not possible within the present system prevailing in India.
It can only take place after a revolution, following a protracted people's struggle ( jan sangharsh ), rising above caste and religion, led by modern minded leaders, in which tremendous sacrifices will have to be made, and thereafter creating a political and social order under which there is rapid industrialization, and steady rise in the standard of living of the people.
https://t.co/fMtvUccqa7
How to launch such a people's struggle which will culminate in a historical people's revolution, is what our patriotic youth should think of, instead of just shouting and screaming at Jantar Mantar
https://t.co/0pTT7mDVQl

インド「ゴキブリ人民党（CJP）」の由来を徹底深掘り
先日のYahoo!ニュース投稿で話題になったように、2026年7月25日、インドの教育相ダルメンドラ・プラダン氏が辞任しました。
これを主導したのが、「ゴキブリ人民党」（英語：Cockroach Janta Party、略称CJP）という風刺的な運動体です。
一見シュールな名前ですが、その由来と急成長の背景には、インドの若者たちが抱える深刻な不満と、SNS時代ならではのユーモア戦略が凝縮されています。
以下で、発端から最近の成果までを詳しく掘り下げます。
1. きっかけとなった「最高裁長官の一言」（2026年5月15日）
すべてはここから始まりました。
インド最高裁判所長官のスーリヤ・カント氏が法廷で、失業中の若者や政府批判をする若者を
「ゴキブリ（cockroaches）」や「寄生虫」と表現したと報じられました（本人は「偽の学位を持つ人々を指したもので、若者全体を侮蔑したわけではない」と後日釈明）。
これに激怒したのが、当時米国在住の30歳インド人男性アビジート・ディプケ氏でした。
How Abhijeet Dipke became the face of India's first Gen Z protest movement  - The Japan Times

2. 創設者アビジート・ディプケ氏とは？
30歳（2026年時点）
ボストン大学出身
以前は野党アーム・アードミ党（AAP）のソーシャルメディアチームで活動経験あり（政治コミュニケーション・ストラテジスト）
2026年5月時点で米国在住（その後抗議のため一時帰国）
彼は5月16日、X（旧Twitter）にこう投稿しました：
「全てのゴキブリが集まったとしたらどうなるだろうか？」
その直後、「ゴキブリ人民党（Cockroach Janta Party）」のSNSアカウントと公式サイト（https://t.co/ykiH8BKTk6）を開設。Googleフォームで「党員募集」を開始しました。

3. 党名の由来 ― ただのジョークではない緻密なパロディ
名称の由来は2重構造になっています：
BJPのもじり
与党インド人民党（Bharatiya Janata Party = BJP）を意識的にパロディ化。「Janta（人民）」をそのまま使い、CJPとした。
「ゴキブリ」という言葉の逆転利用
最高裁長官が使った侮蔑語を、自ら名乗ることで毒を抜き、団結の象徴に転換した。
ゴキブリのイメージ（どんな過酷な環境でも生き残る強靭さ）を「若者のレジリエンス（回復力）」に重ねた、非常に洗練された自己卑下ユーモアです。
公式には「若者による、若者のための、若者の政治組織」と位置づけられ、「入党条件は失業者または怠け者」とジョークを交えています（もちろん本気の登録政党ではありません）。

4. 爆発的な拡大の背景
設立からわずか数週間でInstagramフォロワーが2,200万人超に到達。与党BJPの公式アカウントを上回る勢いでした。

へぇ〜ポイント：
インドは世界最大級の若年人口を抱える一方で、若年失業率が深刻。
2026年もNEET（全国共通医学部入試）の試験問題漏洩や、CBSE（中央中等教育委員会）のオンライン採点システム不具合が相次ぎ、数百万人の学生の将来が脅かされた。
これらの不満が「ゴキブリ」という象徴を通じて一気に結集した。

5. オンラインから街頭へ、そして教育相辞任へ
2026年6月6日：ディプケ氏が米国から帰国し、ニューデリーで初の街頭抗議集会を実施（ジャンタル・マンタルで）。
その後、全国規模の座り込み抗議やデモに発展。
抗議の象徴として「金属の皿をスプーンで叩く」パフォーマンスが行われましたが、これは2020年のCOVID禍でモディ首相が呼びかけた「ターリー・バジャオ（皿を叩いて医療従事者を応援）」のパロディでもありました。
そして2026年7月25日、ついに教育相プラダン氏が辞任を表明。CJPは「要求が実現した」として抗議運動の終了を宣言しました。

まとめ：これは「ただのジョーク政党」ではなかった
CJPは公式に登録された政党ではなく、風刺とミームから生まれたGen Z主導の抗議運動です。しかし、その影響力は本物の政治的成果（教育相辞任）を生み出しました。

へぇ〜な事実まとめ：
党のマスコット画像の多くはAI生成。
Xアカウントは一時「国家安全保障上の懸念」でインド国内からアクセス不能にされたが、後日解除。
「ゴキブリ」という最悪の侮蔑語を、最強の結束の象徴に変えた言語戦略の勝利。
この事例は、SNS時代における若者の政治参加の新しい形を世界に示したと言えます。インドの若者たちが「声を出せば変わる」と実感した瞬間でもありました。
もっと詳しく知りたい部分（例：抗議の具体的な手法、ディプケ氏の過去、またはインドの試験制度の闇など）があれば、教えてください！ さらに深掘りします🐹

body:
From One Word to a Nationwide Protest and Education Minister's Resignation, It all began with a single word COCKROACH 🪳 

​After CJI Suryakant allegedly referred to the youth as "cockroaches," the remark triggered outrage across social media. What many viewed as an insult was transformed into a symbol of resistance, leading to the formation of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP). Instead of rejecting the label, thousands and later millions embraced it

​Supporters claim that more than 26 million people eventually joined or supported the movement online. What started as a reaction to one controversial remark soon grew into a nationwide campaign demanding accountability and reforms.

​The movement reached a new phase at Jantar Mantar, where students protested over alleged paper leaks. Hunger strikes followed, and as tensions escalated, protesters organized a Sansad March. The march ended in clashes with security forces, with reports of a police lathi-charge and over 100 students reportedly injured.

​As the protests spread across the country, pressure on the government continued to mount. Prime Minister Narendra Modi later released his first public video after the NEET paper leak controversy, but many protesters believed the response had come too late.

​And finally, 83 days after the NEET paper leak and 35 days into the ongoing protests, Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned.

​Whether seen as a victory for student activism or simply a political consequence of mounting pressure, the resignation became one of the defining moments of the movement.

​From one word... to a nationwide protest... to a Union Minister's resignation.

body:
The Turning Points That Forced Dharmendra Pradhan’s Resignation

@Cockroachisback , @abhijeet_dipke, @Wangchuk66 , @prakashraaj ,  @AzmiShabana, @SauravDassss 

▶️NEET paper leaks and other exam paper leaks caused endless suffering to lakhs of students. More than 20 students died by suicide due to the NEET paper leak alone.

▶️ CJI called the youth “cockroaches.”  

▶️Abhijeet Dipke from Boston, USA launched the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) online.  

▶️Arun Arora (AAP supporter) in a fun way assigned CJP roles to several known AAP faces. 
 
▶️These volunteers gave the first big push and started trending songs.  

▶️ CJP exploded on Instagram - accounts repeatedly withheld/paused - yet crossed 22 million followers.  

▶️ Abhijeet Dipke announced he was coming to India for the first Jantar Mantar protest (6 June 2026). 
 
▶️ CJP named official spokespersons: Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka, Vijeta Dahiya.  

▶️First Jantar Mantar protest became a massive success. Prakash Raj and Sonam Wangchuk joined, demanding Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation.  

▶️ Protests spread to Pune, Lucknow, Amritsar, Hyderabad, Jaipur and more. Sonam Wangchuk and Prakash Raj kept showing up.  

▶️Opposition parties extended support: AAP, SP, Shiv Sena (UBT), TMC, DMK and others.  

▶️CJP began its indefinite sit-in at Jantar Mantar on 20 June 2026.  

▶️Sonam Wangchuk started his hunger strike at Jantar Mantar on 28 June, demanding Pradhan’s resignation.  Along with him, several students including @neha_aisa too started hunger strike at the site

▶️Student support for CJP grew organically across India.  

▶️ On the 21st day of his hunger strike, police forcibly shifted Sonam Wangchuk to hospital against his will.  

▶️That single mis-step backfired. Support exploded at Jantar Mantar and protests erupted nationwide.  

▶️CJP announced the March to Parliament on 20 July. 2.5 lakh students turned up.  

▶️The entire nation watched in shock as Delhi Police launched a brutal lathi-charge — nails on lathis, RAF pellet guns, shock batons.  

▶️International media extensively covered the police brutality while much of the Indian media ran propaganda branding students as “anti-national.”  

▶️93 former senior civil servants (including a former NSA, former Election Commissioner and former Lt. Governor of Delhi) wrote to the PM condemning the police action.  

▶️ The government thought force would break the movement. Instead, Gen Z became unstoppable.  

▶️ Rahul Gandhi and Congress leaders protested outside the PMO on 21 July.  

▶️People from across India began ordering food and supplies for the protesting students.  

▶️ CJP and AAP launched helplines and secured the release of detained protesters.  Arvind Kejriwal himself went police station after station and got students released. 

▶️Even after being shifted to hospital, Sonam Wangchuk continued his fast. The High Court ordered his transfer to a hospital of his choice (Medanta), yet police still blocked visitors and opposition MPs.  

▶️ On the 26th day, Sonam Wangchuk broke his fast only after receiving written assurances from the Modi government (no FIRs against peaceful protesters, compensation for NEET-related suicide families, and a parliamentary discussion on exam accountability), read out by a BJP minister.  

▶️Nationwide protests on 24 July — “Every district, one day, one demand.”  

▶️The government kept shutting 18 metro stations near Jantar Mantar and blocking roads, punishing ordinary citizens.  

▶️On 25 July, Dharmendra Pradhan resigned.  
The entire nation erupted in joy.

#India’s ‘#Cockroach’ youth movement calls off protests after education minister resigns 

India’s youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has called off its nationwide protests after Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned amid mounting anger over alleged examination paper leaks and irregularities.

The resignation on Saturday followed weeks of demonstrations, including a prolonged sit-in at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar, demanding accountability over the conduct of major national examinations, particularly the NEET-UG medical entrance test. The protests also drew support from activists and opposition figures and spread to other cities.

The CJP, which began as a satirical online movement in May, evolved into a broader youth protest platform focused on exam reforms, unemployment and government accountability. Its demonstrations intensified after alleged examination irregularities triggered widespread frustration among students and families.

According to the Associated Press and The Guardian, the movement declared victory after Pradhan’s resignation and said it would end its main protests following government assurances on key demands, including compensation for affected families, reforms to prevent exam leaks and protection for peaceful protesters from legal action.

Local media reported the resignation marks a significant political setback for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government, coming after sustained public pressure over the education system and examination integrity.

In India, something magnificent happened when young people turned a harsh insult into a historic political victory.

✅During a Supreme Court hearing on May 15, 2026, Chief Justice of India Surya Kant was reprimanding a lawyer over activist litigation. In his remarks, he compared unemployed young people and activists to "COCKROACHES" and "PARASITES of society" who attack state institutions when they fail to find jobs.

✅Instead of slinking away, 30-year-old political communications strategist Abhijeet Dipke launched an online movement the next day called the COCKROACH JANTA PARTY (CJP). Parodying the ruling party (BJP), the CJP adopted the humble cockroach as a mascot, a symbol of resilience, endurance and survival.

✅The movement went viral instantly. Within two weeks, CJP’s Instagram page amassed over 20 million followers, outpacing the official accounts of India’s main political parties.

✅The Boiling Point: Exam Scandals:
The satire transformed into a massive real-world protest when paper leaks invalidated major competitive national entrance exams (such as NEET-UG). Millions of students saw years of hard work shattered.

✅The youth took to the streets, occupying New Delhi’s Jantar Mantar and organizing nationwide sit-ins. Renowned environmentalist and education activist Sonam Wangchuk  joined forces with the youth, embarking on a 26-day hunger strike. The movement set a single non-negotiable demand: 

❌the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan❌

✅On July 25, 2026, after sustained nationwide pressure, Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan officially submitted his resignation to Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

✅Why this was historic: 
Prime Minister Modi's administration has long maintained a strongman image, famously refusing to force or accept minister resignations during major public protests. The youth movement achieved a political concession that few thought possible.

🚨CJP Ends 37-Day Protest After Government Accepts Key Demands, Raising New Questions for India's Democracy

The 37-day nationwide protest led by the CJP formally came to an end after a joint press conference with government representatives, where the organisation announced that its primary objectives had been achieved and instructed protesters to vacate Jantar Mantar and return home peacefully.

According to CJP leaders, the movement was built around three core demands: the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, the withdrawal of FIRs filed against protesters and organisers, and financial compensation for families who allegedly lost loved ones following the NEET paper leak controversy.

The first demand was fulfilled with Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation. The government also reportedly assured the protesters that FIRs related to the agitation would be withdrawn and that future legal action against peaceful participants would not be pursued. On compensation, the government is said to have agreed to provide the maximum assistance permissible under existing provisions to affected families. CJP stated that these assurances were made in writing, prompting it to withdraw the agitation in what it described as an act of "good faith."

The protest's conclusion marks a significant political moment. It is being viewed as one of the rare instances in recent years where sustained public mobilisation coincided with the resignation of a Union minister. While the opposition had consistently demanded the minister's removal inside Parliament, much of the political credit is likely to be associated with the street movement rather than parliamentary pressure.

At the same time, the government's reported assurance to withdraw FIRs has sparked debate over its long-term implications. Critics argue that withdrawing cases linked to a mass protest could establish a precedent that future movements, regardless of their nature, may seek to invoke. They contend that allegations involving violence or damage to public property are ordinarily expected to be addressed through the judicial process rather than political negotiations. Supporters, however, maintain that many protesters faced legal action despite participating peacefully and believe the withdrawal is necessary to prevent unnecessary criminalisation of dissent.

During the course of the protest, concerns were also raised over misinformation circulating on social media, including claims that several foreign and Pakistani-linked accounts amplified misleading narratives surrounding the movement. While such allegations became part of the public discourse, there has been no conclusive evidence to suggest that they altered the overall course of the agitation.

With the protest now officially withdrawn, attention is expected to shift back to Parliament, where several important legislative measures remain pending. The episode leaves behind a lasting political and constitutional debate over the role of protests, government accountability, legal processes, and the future relationship between street activism and democratic institutions.

The 2021 NEET-PG counselling movement was one of the biggest nationwide protests by resident doctors in India.

Led by the 𝙁𝙚𝙙𝙚𝙧𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣 𝙤𝙛 𝙍𝙚𝙨𝙞𝙙𝙚𝙣𝙩 𝘿𝙤𝙘𝙩𝙤𝙧𝙨' 𝘼𝙨𝙨𝙤𝙘𝙞𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣 (𝙁𝙊𝙍𝘿𝘼) along with other resident doctors' associations, thousands of doctors across India protested against the prolonged delay in NEET-PG counselling and admissions.

At that time, the 𝙐𝙣𝙞𝙤𝙣 𝙃𝙚𝙖𝙡𝙩𝙝 𝙈𝙞𝙣𝙞𝙨𝙩𝙚𝙧 𝙬𝙖𝙨 𝙈𝙖𝙣𝙨𝙪𝙠𝙝 𝙈𝙖𝙣𝙙𝙖𝙫𝙞𝙮𝙖. The doctors demanded immediate counselling, timely recruitment of new residents, and relief from the excessive workload caused by the shortage of doctors in hospitals.

The protest intensified in December 2021, with demonstrations across the country and disruption of services in several government hospitals. Representatives of FORDA and other doctors' bodies held discussions with the Health Ministry, after which assurances were given to expedite the counselling process.

Following the government's assurances and the Supreme Court proceedings, the resident doctors called off their strike in January 2022, while continuing to monitor the implementation of the commitments.

This movement highlighted the vital role of resident doctors in India's healthcare system and the need for timely medical recruitment and better healthcare planning.

After weeks of protests, sleepless nights and a march to Parliament, the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) has finally called off its agitation at Delhi's Jantar Mantar.

The announcement came after a fresh round of talks with the Centre, with the government agreeing to the movement's key demands, including the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. CJP leaders then appealed to supporters to peacefully disperse and begin returning home, saying the protest had achieved its objective.

The mood at Jantar Mantar changed almost instantly.

The roads around the protest site, which had witnessed barricades, police deployment and tense stand-offs over the past several weeks, turned into scenes of celebration. Supporters danced to music, chanted slogans, showered flower petals, embraced one another and celebrated what they described as a victory for the student movement. Drums, songs and cheers echoed through the streets surrounding Jantar Mantar as thousands marked the end of the agitation.

The Centre has also agreed to several other demands raised by the movement, including measures related to examination reforms, compensation for families of students whose deaths the movement linked to NEET, withdrawal of cases against peaceful protesters and assurances that no action would be taken against students who participated in the demonstrations.

Opposition parties, which had backed the protests over the past several weeks, welcomed the developments while maintaining that the police action during the 20 July crackdown must also be accounted for.

After more than a month, the protest site that became the epicentre of one of the country's biggest student-led movements is finally beginning to empty—but only after ending on a celebratory note.

The Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) has officially called off its protest at Jantar Mantar following discussions with government representatives.

This comes after Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan submitted his resignation earlier in the day. 

Speaking after a meeting at the Constitution Club of India, CJP leaders announced that the protest would not continue for now while also presenting a five-point charter outlining their remaining demands. 

These include compensation for families of students who died by suicide in connection with the NEET paper leak controversy, the release of detained students and protesters, and no fresh FIRs against those involved.

From the ground, people were seen leaving the protest site as metro stations reopened, though some participants continued to express support for the movement and its demands.

🌈 My thoughts on the NEET protest :

📎 1. I have stayed largely silent on the NEET agitation out of deference to those closer to events. My concern has been less political and more about the need for lasting examination reform.

📎2. It is welcome that the Government has engaged with the students' concerns and responded with empathy to key demands.

📎3. Credit is also due to the CJP and its leadership for keeping the movement largely restrained and articulate despite strong criticism from different people and TV anchors.

📎4. The next challenge is implementation. A law alone is not enough; it must be backed by a time-bound investigation that fixes accountability and restores public trust.

📎5. Dr. Radhakrishnan's 2024 recommendations after the first NEET leak were sound. The question in 2026 is not what more needs to be recommended, but why those recommendations were not implemented.

📎6. Basic questions remain unanswered. Who selected the paper setters, from what pool, under what SOP, and who approved those selections? These answers should not have to wait for fresh recruitment into the NTA. They should already be known and made public. Because it matters more than nabbing the  leakers.

📎7. In 2024, the breach involved tampering with question paper boxes. In 2026, it appears to involve an insider leak linked to paper setters. If so, identifying the approval chain is critical to determine whether the failure arose from negligence, incompetence or corruption.

📎8. Finally, the use of lathis, indiscriminate RAF firing, and organised stone-pelting at protest sites all deserve condemnation. In a democracy, neither excessive force nor organised violence is acceptable. The real test is whether this crisis produces a more credible examination system and a more mature handling of public order.

I hope one can see changes which show on the ground - not only in courtrooms and behind closed doors.  meetings

STORY | CJP calls off protest as government accepts all demands

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on Saturday withdrew its agitation over the NEET issue after the government accepted all demands of the outfit, including the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan and withdrawal of FIRs against protesters.

The announcement came following talks between the two sides soon after Pradhan said on X that he has sent his resignation to the prime minister.

Union Minister JP Nadda said the government will give "honourable compensation" within rules to the families of the students who committed suicide after the NEET test cancellation and ensure withdrawal of all FIRs registered against the protesters.

"As the government accepted all our demands, we call off our protests with immediate effect. We appeal to everyone to go back home peacefully," CJP's spokesperson Saurav Das said at a joint press conference with Nadda and Union Minister Jitendra Singh.

The CJP has led a sit-in at Jantar Mantar since June 20, demanding accountability over the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak and irregularities in the CBSE's on-screen marking process, besides seeking wider reforms in the conduct of public examinations.

The agitation has galvanised thousands of students in protests across the country and has been supported by major opposition parties.

Jantar Mantar Agitation Withdrawn as Centre Accedes to Key Demands! 
The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has officially announced the end of its multi-week protest at Delhi's Jantar Mantar following the third round of high-level negotiations with a central government delegation comprising Union Ministers J.P. Nadda and Jitendra Singh.  Speaking at a joint press conference, CJP National Spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka confirmed that the agitation was called off after the government accepted its core demands, starting with the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. In addition to the minister's exit, the Centre agreed to:
- Withdraw all FIRs and legal cases registered against protesting students and organizers, guaranteeing no future retaliatory action.  
- Provide maximum financial compensation under regulatory provisions to the families of NEET aspirants who died by suicide amid the examination controversy.  
- Consider the 5-point charter on examination system reforms submitted by the student leaders.  
- CJP spokespersons urged all student protesters to vacate the venue peacefully and return home as the government pledged to honor its commitments in good faith.  

#CJPProtest #JantarMantar #DharmendraPradhan #NEET #StudentVictory

Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation was a calculated political move to de-escalate manufactured chaos, not some grand victory for the so-called “people’s movement.” 

Sonam Wangchuk never demanded anyone’s head he ended his hunger strike after assurances, showing pragmatism.

Yet CJP’s Abhijit Dipke and his outfit refuse to back down, desperately clinging to their agitation because their real agenda was never just NEET reforms it was political disruption and scoring points against a strong government.

This isn’t student advocacy; it’s selective outrage and opportunistic politics dressed up as protest.

While genuine concerns over exam leaks deserve accountability and systemic fixes, CJP’s refusal to accept reality exposes their hypocrisy.

Pradhan served with dedication on education reforms; bowing to sustained pressure doesn’t erase his contributions or validate endless vendettas. 

Wangchuk moved on why can’t Dipke and CJP? 

Their agitation was always more about optics and pressure tactics than solutions.

Time to focus on real governance, not performative politics that hold India’s youth hostage.

धर्मेंद्र प्रधान का इस्तीफ़ा बताता है कि देश में छात्रों, युवाओं और GenZ के संघर्ष ने अहंकारी – तानाशाही मोदी सरकार को झुका दिया।
राष्ट्रपति जी को अब तुरंत प्रभाव से यह इस्तीफ़ा स्वीकार कर लेना चाहिए।

राहुल गांधी जी के नेतृत्व में कांग्रेस पार्टी पिछले कई साल से सड़क से लेकर संसद तक education system में सुधार के समर्थन और Paper Leak के विरोध में आवाज़ उठा रही है। मुझे गर्व है कि इस आंदोलन में भी @INCIndia पार्टी ने ज़िम्मेदार विपक्ष की भूमिका निभाई।

‘छात्रों की गूंज’ के तहत देश के स्टूडेंट्स को एकजुट किया, प्रधान मंत्री आवास के बाहर मजबूती के साथ धरना दिया गया, LOp को पुलिस हिरासत में लिया गया और कांग्रेस, @nsui, @IYC सहित हमारे सभी संगठनों ने पूरी मजबूती के साथ इस लड़ाई को लड़ा।

NEET Paper Leak के बाद से Congress Party इस मांग पर डटी रही कि education minister के resignation से कम कुछ मंजूर नहीं है। @RahulGandhi जी ने आज सुबह भी कहा था कि नरेंद्र मोदी अब इस देश का अतीत बन चुके हैं, हमारे ये बच्चे और स्टूडेंट्स देश का भविष्य हैं और अतीत कभी भविष्य को नहीं हरा सकता।

जिस तरह से जंतर मंतर पर महीने भर से अधिक समय से देश भर के students इकट्ठे हुए, GenZ एकजुट हुए, innovative और शांतिपूर्ण तरीके से इस सड़ी हुई व्यवस्था के खिलाफ़ अपना आक्रोश जाहिर किया। इस पूरे दौरान CJP और तमाम संगठनों, विपक्षी दलों ने जो एकजुटता दिखाई; वह काबिल-ए-तारीफ़ है। देशभर की छात्रशक्ति के collective efforts से इस शासन का घमंड टूटा है।

20 जुलाई 2026 का दिन फिर भी कभी भुलाया नहीं जाएगा। जिस तरह से देश के बच्चों पर, GenZ पर सरकार की शय पर बर्बरता की गई, लाठीचार्ज किया गया, आँसू गैस के गोले दागे गए, पैलेट गन चलाई गई, वह सब मोदी सरकार का एक अक्षम्य अपराध है, जिसे कभी माफ़ नहीं किया जाएगा।

छात्रों के आंदोलन को कुचलने के लिए इस सरकार ने क्या कुछ नहीं किया ?
पूरी दिल्ली को एक तरह से lock कर दिया, 17 - 18 मेट्रो स्टेशन बंद कर दिए, जंतर मंतर और आसपास कई किलोमीटर तक internet बंद कर दिया, पुलिस की सख्ती बढ़ा दी गई और इन दिनों तो protest site पर food और water delivery भी रोक दी गई थी। यह खुले तौर पर देशवासियों के fundamental rights और human rights पर हमला है।

20 जुलाई को छात्रों के साथ जो हिंसा की गई, उसकी जाँच की जानी चाहिए, ज़िम्मेदारी तय की जाए। गृह मंत्री और प्रधान मंत्री इस देश से अपने कुकर्मों के लिए माफ़ी मांगे। संसद में शिक्षा व्यवस्था में सुधारों पर सकारात्मक रूप से चर्चा की जाए और पेपर लीक के तनाव के कारण देश के जिन होनहार स्टूडेंट्स ने अपनी जान दे दी, उनके परिवारों की मदद की जाए।

देश के युवाओं, GenZ और स्टूडेंट्स के समर्थन में, education system को सुधारने के लिए हमारा संघर्ष हमेशा जारी रहेगा।✊🏻

Instagram algorithm won.
Everyone knows there are cameras and media at the protests. 
An opportunity for reels, likes, followers pay-out. They wanted that, and they got it.

Talk about the guy who made the Woo Woo video, then posted another celebrating 150K followers. Scroll his account it’s full of content about going viral celebrating his reach, not NEET. Or the girl standing in front of the van who wants  to become a global actress. Or the girls in deep neck sarees and tees.

Dipke knew this. His own Vijeta Dahiya and Arpit Sharma are reel makers. They knew their playground already. The easiest way to pull Gen Z into the streets was through Instagram where every moment could become a reel.

Look closely. The videos getting the most likes from the CJP protest are from influencers(not students) whose next videos are about hitting 100M views or 100K followers overnight and not about the NEET exam.

Just like TikTok..BJP needs to find a reason to ban Instagram and these reel making platforms so students can concentrate on studies/exams instead of chasing viral fame in protests.

At least hoping that each and every vandal, abuser and content whore will be held accountable as well, FIRs will be lodged and they are added to the national criminal databases.

Surrendering to pressure only feeds lawlessness. You might buy a little breathing space as this protest fades, but you have handed agitators another win. They will be back stronger next time.

Hope you are ready. @bip4india

पोरं जिंकली, Dhamendra Pradhan यांचा राजीनामा, Narendra Modi सरकार बॅकफूटवर 

नरेंद्र मोदींच्या १२ वर्षांच्या कार्यकाळात जे घडलं नाही, ते आज कालच्या तरुणांनी करून दाखवलं आहे! केंद्रीय शिक्षणमंत्री धर्मेंद्र प्रधान यांनी अखेर आपल्या पदाचा राजीनामा दिला आहे. NEET पेपरफुटी प्रकरण, विद्यार्थ्यांच्या आत्महत्या आणि भवितव्याशी झालेला खेळ याविरोधात 'कॉकरोच जनता पार्टी' (CJP), GenZ आणि देशभरातील विद्यार्थ्यांनी दिल्लीच्या जंतर-मंतरवर सलग ३५ दिवस ऐतिहासिक आंदोलन केले. पर्यावरण कार्यकर्ते सोनम वांगचूक यांचे उपोषण, राहुल गांधींचा पाठिंबा आणि विद्यार्थ्यांवर झालेला लाठीचार्ज या सगळ्यानंतर सरकारला अखेर नमावे लागले. धर्मेंद्र प्रधान यांनी आपल्या राजीनाम्याच्या पत्रात नक्की काय म्हटले आहे? CJP चे संस्थापक अभिजित दीपके आणि तरुणांनी हा विजय कसा मिळवला? जाणून घ्या या सविस्तर व्हिडिओमध्ये!

History has been made! In an unprecedented move during PM Narendra Modi's 12-year tenure, Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan has resigned. What seasoned politicians couldn't achieve, the youth of India—Gen Z and the 'Cockroach Janta Party' (CJP)—made possible. Following the massive NEET-UG paper leak scam, ruined careers, and a 35-day relentless protest at Jantar Mantar, the Modi government was forced to bow down. Supported by climate activist Sonam Wangchuk's 26-day fast and Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, the student movement led by CJP founder Abhijit Dipke faced lathi charges but refused to back down.

body: One thing that I can vouch for is GOI is NOT chutiya, there is a contingency plan! Also, If you do an indept analysis of the letter from Dharmendra Pradhan you will observe that the document is designed as a trap for the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) rather than a straightforward concession. By publishing the text directly as unformatted image cards on social media without an official letterhead, seal or wet-ink signature, Pradhan has successfully bypassed traditional bureaucratic routing to execute a populist maneuver. This lack of institutional insignia is a calculated tactical choice that transforms an administrative exit into an unfiltered emotional appeal directly to the public base. The text front-loads administrative accountability by meticulously detailing the May 3 NEET-UG disruptions, the subsequent CBI investigation, the June 21 re-examination, and the structural pivot to Computer-Based Testing (CBT), thereby establishing a preemptive defense that the state moved swiftly to correct system failures. By pivoting to complain that individuals in responsible positions created hurdles following the July 16 results, the narrative introduces an ambiguous villain that shifts public anger away from the ministry itself. The core of the trap for the CJP lies in the text's explicit invocation of the protests at Jantar Mantar and its warning against anti-national forces. By framing the resignation as an altruistic sacrifice designed to keep student futures out of legal complexities and to neutralize national security vulnerabilities the document acts as tactical jujitsu against the movement. It presents the CJP leadership with a severe strategic dilemma if the movement declares victory and demobilizes, it loses its momentum, but if it stays on the streets to push secondary demands, state and media apparatuses can reframe the protest as an intractable, politically motivated disruption rather than a student-led welfare campaign.

body:
First, let's give the students their due. 

They pushed, and a Union minister is gone. That does not happen often in this country.

Dharmendra Pradhan has resigned as Education Minister today, sending his letter to the Prime Minister, in the middle of the nationwide protests over the NEET-UG paper leak. 

This came just hours after reports that the government was only planning to shift him to another ministry. 

So the street did the resignation.

This is a pattern with this government.

When the farmers sat on Delhi's borders for a year, the three farm laws were repealed. When the lateral entry recruitment ad drew backlash in 2024, it was pulled. And now, after weeks of protest, a minister has stepped down.

Say what you want about the politics. A government that climbs down when the public pushes hard enough is democracy actually working. 

The pressure is supposed to travel upward like this. And given the chaos, stepping him down was the right call.

The protests had shut 18 Delhi Metro stations and brought real disruption to the capital, with students at Jantar Mantar and Sonam Wangchuk on a hunger strike. 

When a situation is that hot, removing the lightning rod cools it fast. It buys everyone room to breathe.

But, to be honest, a resignation solves almost nothing about the actual problem.

Remember how this leak even happened. The paper did not walk out of a broken vault. It came from an insider, a subject expert the NTA itself had appointed, who recalled the questions and passed them on. 

A new minister in the chair does not touch that. He does not change the press, the storage room, or the panel of experts who see the paper before the students do.

And we already learned that a tough law alone does not stop this. The anti-paper-leak law with ten-year jail terms was on the books in 2024. The paper still leaked in 2026. Punishment on paper did not prevent it.

So if the resignation is the headline, the actual solution is the Centre is moving NEET to a computer-based test format from next year. 

It has set up an STF and fast-track courts with day-to-day trials, and it has proposed seven key amendments to the anti-paper-leak law. This sits on top of the earlier steps, the CBI probe, the cancelled exam, and the re-test whose results came on 16 July.

A computer-based test with a secure, randomised question bank is far harder to leak than a single printed paper trucked to thousands of centres. 

But the 2024 law was announced too, and it failed in practice. So the only thing worth watching now is execution. 

> Does the CBT rollout actually stay secure.
> Do the fast-track courts hand down real sentences. 
> Does the expert-selection process genuinely change. 

Announcements are easy but none of them stop a leak by themselves.

Two more honest things;

This was late. Pradhan's resignation was being demanded back in the 2024 NEET row, by opposition parties and student groups alike. 

He did not go then. It took a second leak, a bigger crisis, and a student movement on the streets to force it now. 

And it did not even end the protest. The CJP called it a partial victory and laid out two more demands before they stop, a one crore compensation for the families of students who died by suicide during this crisis, and disciplinary action against the police for the force used on protesters on 20 July. 

In my opinion, the only number that actually matters is whether a paper leaks next May. 

If the CBT shift and the court cases and the NTA overhaul are done properly, this becomes a real turning point. If they stay as press notes, we will be back here in two years with a new minister and the same hole in the wall.

The reform is the test.

“We are cockroaches; once it enters, it does not leave.”

Following the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the NEET-UG paper leak controversy, Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke made it clear at Jantar Mantar that the student movement is far from over.

Addressing the crowd after news of the minister's exit broke, Dipke emphasized that while Pradhan's resignation marks a massive victory for student accountability, the CJP will not clear the protest site until its remaining key demands are met—including ₹1 crore compensation for the families of students who died by suicide amid exam stress, and full accountability for police actions during earlier demonstrations.

Will Total Filth, Vulgarity, And Abuse Qualify As Protest? 

We pose a crucial question to the country: Can utter filth, vulgarity, and insults ever be deemed an acceptable form of democratic protest? After our extensive investigation into the significant devastation and heaps of waste left at Jantar Mantar by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), we are now revealing the alarming behavioral truth of these so-called student leaders.

Here is the direct, unfiltered footage that highlights the harsh slogans and the shocking behavior of the demonstrators. The constitutional assurance of peaceful protest exists in this nation, but does that revered right allow for public vandalism and offensive language?

CNN-News18 Exclusive | A Delhi Police surveillance exercise using facial recognition technology and crime database matching has identified 2,873 people with criminal records among those who participated in the July 20 CJP-led student protest at Jantar Mantar during the Parliament March, according to findings accessed by CNN-News18.

Police records show 989 individuals had serious criminal antecedents, including those facing murder, attempted murder, robbery, dacoity, snatching, Arms Act, NDPS, rape, molestation and POCSO cases. Investigators say many were repeat offenders, with several having multiple criminal cases against them.

According to police sources, the findings have raised concerns that organised criminal elements may have infiltrated what was projected as a peaceful student demonstration, increasing the risk of violence, vandalism and threats to public safety. Officials also flagged the presence of accused linked to crimes against women and children as a major concern in a crowded protest setting.

CJP is celebrating the resignation of the Education Minister as some great "victory."

But ask them one simple question—how does one man's resignation fix systemic exam leaks or create a foolproof system?

They have no answer.

Most of them don't even know about the Radhakrishnan Committee or its recommendations. Why? Because they never wanted real, long-term solutions. They only wanted a political scalp.

This entire protest was never about education reform. It was a carefully orchestrated, politically motivated agitation backed by AAP, certain extremists, and the usual left-liberal gang whose only real agenda is to abuse Modi day and night.

Vulgar language, open hate, and pure political opportunism dressed up as student anger.

Resignation is not the solution. Structural reform is. And these people were never interested in that.

Here's the accurate data on the number of medical colleges and MBBS seats in India:

In 2014: • 387 medical colleges • 51,348 MBBS seats

In 2026: • 844 medical colleges • 1,39,489 MBBS seats

The number of medical colleges has more than doubled.

MBBS seats have nearly tripled.

This is real capacity building—not just slogans or protests demanding resignations.

While some are busy shouting for political optics, the actual expansion of medical education has been historic.

While you are criticising the government for not doing anything, you should first look at the numbers above.

Now let's come to the main argument.

According to me, the Education Minister should resign not because the NEET paper leak happened, as he had no direct role in it. It was carried out by paper setters and the coaching mafia.

However, he should resign for not implementing the Radhakrishnan Committee's recommendations in full.

The Radhakrishnan Committee's 101 recommendations are more than an anti-paper leak roadmap—they're a blueprint to rebuild trust in India's examination system.

Key reforms include:

🔹 Encrypted digital question paper delivery, printed only minutes before the exam.

🔹 Aadhaar + biometric + AI-based multi-stage candidate verification to curb impersonation.

🔹 AI-driven detection of cheating, suspicious score patterns, and malpractice.

🔹 Around 1,000 secure government testing centres with CCTV, mobile jammers, and standardised infrastructure.

🔹 Gradual shift to Computer-Based and Adaptive Testing.

🔹 Stronger cybersecurity, reduced outsourcing, dedicated vigilance and research wings, better grievance redressal, and mental health support.

The committee correctly identified that paper leaks aren't isolated failures—they're symptoms of systemic weaknesses across the entire exam lifecycle.

The solution, therefore, isn't just harsher punishment; it's structural reform through technology, governance, and accountability.

If implemented effectively, these reforms could significantly reduce paper leaks, improve transparency, restore public confidence, and modernise the examination process for the 2+ crore students who appear for competitive exams every year.

Now the real challenge is ensuring these recommendations move from paper to practice.

📢 Saurav Das (@SauravDassss) ,you’ve been covering law & courts for a while now. 

➡ No law degree? Fine. 

➡ The Supreme Court has every authority to pass any order in proceedings before, especially when fundamental rights are allegedly violated.

➡ Injured police officials are also citizens of India. They too have a right to justice.

➡ If this basic point somehow escaped you, feel free to call your Indira Jaisingh (@indirajsingh) or Kapil Sibal (@KapilSibal). They might still take your call. Afterall, they are funding you.

➡ And why the sudden concern for history-sheeters? Genuine protestors should be superbly relieved by today’s interim order.

➡ Court has told the state: don’t proceed against the protesting crowd. Only those with criminal antecedents face action.

➡ Times of India (@timesofindia) reports, police have already identified over 100 history sheeters, including murder accused, who were part of the crowd.

➡ IS CJP (@Cockroachisback) worried the history sheeters?

➡ Because Delhi Police, in a report submitted to the government, has stated that a total of 2,873 people involved in the CJP (@CJP_for_India) protests at Jantar Mantar were found to have criminal antecedents. Of these, 989 individuals had criminal records involving heinous offences.

➡ The Delhi Police and the government were right take action. 

➡ One can reasonably conclude why the government decided to de-escalate the situation in the interest of larger public safety.

➡ Government of West Bengal issues order:- No coercive measures shall be taken against the students participating in the protests relating to the alleged irregularities in the NEET (UG) Examination.

➡ The above protection shall not extend to persons having criminal antecedents, as mandated in the order of the Hon'ble Supreme Court mentioned above.

Agnipath protests (2022)**: Youth opposed the new short-term military recruitment scheme; opposition parties backed it and the government called the agitation politically motivated.  
Wrestlers’ protest (2023)**: Top athletes demanded action against WFI chief Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh over harassment charges; opposition joined and the sit-in became a national political issue.  
Manipur conflict (2023–ongoing)**: Ethnic grievances over ST status and land rights escalated into prolonged violence with heavy political involvement.  
Ladakh protests (2023–2026)**: Demands for statehood and Sixth Schedule protections, led in part by Sonam Wangchuk, drew sustained political attention.

These follow the same pattern as the 2026 CJP/NEET movement: a focused grievance that attracts political parties and broader framing.

Taking note of a plea on the use of metallic pellet guns during the recent students' protests against the NEET paper leak in Delhi, Supreme Court on Thursday asked Centre to preserve ammunition log of RAF deployed at Jantar Mantar.

Observing that police, as per  Bureau of Police Research and Development (BPRD) advisory, are empowered to use pellet guns in exceptional situations, top court termed “vague” the prayer in the plea seeking a complete ban on such usage.

A bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana took note of submissions of senior advocate Vrinda Grover.

Former Central Information Commissioner and retired IPS officer Yashovardhan Azad and the two victims had moved court seeking a complete ban on use of metallic pellet guns to deal with law and order situations.

At theoutset, Justice Bagchi said that the prayer for a ban on the use of pellet guns by law enforcement agencies for civilian crowd dispersal was "vague" without challenging the police regulations, which permit the use of such weapons.

Grover said it was not easy to find such regulations in the public domain, and urged the bench to direct the Centre to place them on record.

Singh and Mansoori reportedly suffered pellet injuries during the ‘Sansad Chalo’ march called by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) on July 20.

Grover said as regards the petitioners, metallic pellets were used, and they were recovered from their bodies.

“I am not saying pellet guns should not be in the armoury of the RAF or not. Here it is different. They have used metallic pellets,” she said.

The bench said it was not averse to examining the use of pellets in a particular incident and the petitioners must show if it was permissible under a "graded approach".

The senior lawyer said she was confining her reliefs to metallic pellets.

"There is no standing order of the Delhi Police which permits the use of pellets. That is why my difficulty arises, and I have to rely on BPRD. If there is such a standing order, the Union may place it on record. I am sure the Union and the Delhi Police do not wish to fire pellets on innocent youngsters,” she said.

“I could not find any such standing order of the Delhi Police at all," Grover said.

Solicitor General Tushar Mehta said the government will do whatever is necessary to assist the bench.

Grover said the top court on July 28 directed the preservation of CCTV, drone, body camera footage and wireless logs and did not specifically refer to ammunition logs of the RAF.

“Whatever is required for investigation will be preserved,” solicitor general said.

The bench said a bona fide protest may turn violent at any point, perhaps due to the infiltration of anti-social elements, and “graded responses” by law enforcement might sometimes be necessary.

The forces may have to take on the spot decision based on the event, the law officer said.

Yashovardhan Azad approached the top court seeking a nationwide ban on the use of wholly or partly metallic pellet ammunition fired from pump-action or projectile action guns for dispersing civilian assemblies, contending that such weapons are inherently incompatible with constitutional standards governing the use of force.

The petition also sought exemplary compensation, comprehensive medical treatment and rehabilitation for all persons allegedly injured in the incident.

According to petition, RAF, deployed to assist Delhi Police in crowd management during protests, resorted to tear gas, lathi-charge and subsequently fired pump-action guns loaded with metallic pellets near Connaught Place.

The petitioners alleged that no prior warning or announcement was issued before the escalation in use of force and that several protesters suffered serious injuries, including eye injuries.

The promise was that no lawsuits or punitive actions would be taken against students who participated in the protest. The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on Tuesday, July 28, stated that the Supreme Court's interim order permits authorities to continue investigating FIRs registered during the nationwide student protests. The so called party says that the order was contrary to the assurances given by the Centre during negotiations that ended the protests at Jantar Mantar.
“The Supreme Court has now said that FIRs that were already registered will not be withdrawn. This is not what was discussed in our negotiations with the government,” CJP spokesperson Saurav Das said.
CJP has threatened another protest if the order is not withdrawn.

Govt rolls out 'One Officer, One Official Car' rule to curb misuse, cut spending

The government has rolled out a new “One Officer, One Official Car” policy aimed at curbing the misuse of government vehicles and reducing unnecessary expenditure. Under the new rule, officials will be assigned a designated official vehicle instead of multiple cars being used by the same officer or department.
The move is expected to improve accountability, optimise the use of government resources and bring down spending on fuel, maintenance and vehicle operations. It also seeks to discourage the practice of government vehicles being used for personal or non-official purposes.

The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has filed a chargesheet against 13 accused in connection with the alleged NEET-UG 2026 paper leak case, marking a major development in the investigation into irregularities surrounding the medical entrance examination.
The chargesheet reportedly details the alleged roles of the accused and the conspiracy through which the question paper was leaked and subsequently circulated among candidates. The case has raised concerns over the integrity of competitive examinations and the security of the examination system.

13 Indian sailors trapped in the Black Sea near Ukraine amid attacks

Thirteen Indian sailors are reportedly trapped in the Black Sea near Ukraine amid ongoing attacks and heightened security concerns in the region. The sailors are believed to be facing difficulties as military activity and strikes have disrupted maritime operations, raising concerns about their safety and ability to leave the area.

The situation has drawn attention to the risks faced by seafarers operating in conflict-affected waters. Authorities are expected to monitor developments closely and explore options to ensure the sailors’ safe evacuation or passage to a secure location.

Pakistan’s Defense Minister Khawaja Asif defends the killing of protestors in Pakistan-Occupied-Kashmir, says they are enemy like India

Pakistan Occupied Kashmir has been seeing widespread protests for weeks. Islamabad has unleashed unheard of brutality on the protesters, killing them with impunity. Despite the barbarity of the establishment, the protest is only growing.

Now, Pakistan’s Defense Minister Khawaja Asif has tried to justify the murders of the protesters by saying that they are enemies like India.

body:
CJP’s protest exposed something nobody is discussing.
The money.
I asked one simple question.
Who paid for all this?

A few months ago,
Abhijeet Dipke was in the US.

Then came a remark from the Chief Justice.
Then came a meme page.
Then came millions of views.

Then came coordinated amplification.
Bots.
Anonymous pages.
Influencers.

Reels appearing everywhere.

Suddenly, Dipke returned to India.
Permission was secured.

A protest site appeared at Jantar Mantar.
Tents went up.
Stages were built.
Food began arriving.

Then Sonam Wangchuk joined.
Celebrities appeared.
Political leaders followed.
Student wings mobilised.

The crowd grew.
The story changed.

What began as a NEET protest became a political spectacle.

So I stopped watching the videos.
I started calculating the bills.

The protest ran from 6 June to 20 July.
That is 45 days.

45 days of continuous operations.
Let us calculate the economic value.

Food and beverages: ₹13 crore.
Daily transportation: ₹3 crore.
Final-day mobilisation: ₹3 crore.
Stage, tents, sound: ₹2.5 crore.
Water and drinks: ₹2 crore.
Volunteer logistics: ₹1.5 crore.
Accommodation and boarding: ₹3 crore.
Senior legal services: ₹1.5 Crore.
Medical counters and emergency: ₹3 crore.
Banners and printing: ₹2 crore.
PR and digital production: ₹2.5 Crore.
Social-media operations: ₹3.5 crore.
Speakers and invited guests: ₹2.5 crore.
Administration and operations: ₹1.5 crore.
Technical support: ₹0.5 crore.
Contingency: ₹3 crore.
Special Fees: ₹5 Crore.

Subtotal: ~₹52 crore.

Then came 20 July.
Approx 50,000 people turned up.
As per Media.

50,000 people do not materialise from thin air.

They must be contacted.
Transported.
Directed.
Supplied with water.
Managed on the ground.

Another ₹5 crore.

Add the YouTube machinery.
Video teams.
Editors.
Content creators.
Social-media pages.
Real-time amplification.

Another ₹5 crore.

Add the wider digital amplification surrounding the final mobilisation: Another ₹5 crore.

Then came reports and visuals of celebrations and hospitality. Add: ₹1 crore.

The total Cost: ~₹68 crore.

Read that again.
₹68 crore.

This was not a few angry students carrying handmade placards.
This was an operation.

Money leaves fingerprints.
Logistics leave patterns.
Amplification leaves digital trails.

So who funded it?

If I answer that today,
my account may not survive tomorrow.

But one thing is difficult to ignore.
This was not spontaneous.

It was organised.
Resourced.
Planned.

The scale demands questions.
The logistics demand answers.
Someone financed this machinery.

This story is only beginning.

The funding trail is where I am headed next.

Recent assurances by JPNadda & DrJitendraSingh on withdrawing FIRs against peaceful CJP protesters (tied to education issues/NEET) are fresh from July 25 talks, with written guarantees & timelines promised.

I found no prominent, well-documented cases where *these specific leaders* failed to follow through on identical past assurances about dropping protest cases. 

Broader pattern in Indian politics (across parties/govts): 
- Assurances during farmers’ protests, CAA agitations, student movements etc. often led to partial/delayed withdrawals. 
- Reasons: federal structure (state police handle most FIRs), legal processes, probes into alleged violence, or shifting priorities. 
- BJP-ruled states sometimes acted faster on aligned protests; opposition states slower. 

Implementation here starts with FIR copies in days & full withdrawal “shortly.” Public scrutiny on follow-through is fair—politics rewards delivery over promises.

The observation came during hearings on a batch of petitions arising out of the July 20 Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)-led protest at Jantar Mantar over NEET paper leak, during which several demonstrators sustained pellet injuries. Supreme Court's interim order in the NEET protest cases draws a clear distinction between peaceful student protesters and individuals with prior criminal antecedents.

A Bench comprising the Chief Justice of India, Justice Joymalya Bagchi, and Justice V. Mohana directed that investigations into the registered FIRs may continue, but no coercive action shall be taken against protesting students.

At the same time, the Court categorically clarified that this protection will NOT extend to persons with prior criminal antecedents. It also ordered the release of eligible juveniles on simple bonds and directed authorities to preserve CCTV, drone, body-camera and PCR footage from the protest sites.

However, CJP spokesperson Sourav Das publicly objected to this specific condition. Speaking to ANI, he said:

"अगर सुप्रीम कोर्ट बोल रही है कि जिनके ऊपर FIRs हैं पहले से उनको मत छोड़िए, तो वह हमें मंजूर नहीं है..."

This statement raises serious public-interest questions:

• Why oppose the Supreme Court's explicit exclusion of persons with prior criminal antecedents from interim protection?

• If the Court has consciously differentiated between genuine student protesters and those with existing criminal records, should that distinction not be respected?

• Does objecting to this condition undermine the Court's attempt to balance civil liberties with public safety and the rule of law?

The Supreme Court has not barred investigations. It has merely protected eligible students from coercive action while ensuring that those with prior criminal antecedents do not automatically receive the same relief.

The matter is now listed for further hearing on 3 August 2026, when the Union of India, the Government of NCT of Delhi and other concerned States will file their responses.

The debate is no longer just about protests—it is about whether judicial safeguards distinguishing peaceful demonstrators from repeat offenders should be respected.
