Across the streets of New Delhi and industrial hubs throughout Northern India, a vibrant, irreverent, and deeply angry youth movement has erupted into open defiance against Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s far-right Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government. What began as an online meme responding to judicial arrogance has transformed into tens of thousands of students, unemployed workers, and young professionals paralyzing the capital. Calling themselves the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP), these youth have reclaimed an ruling-class insult to build a formidable political force.

Yet, as state repression intensifies and the movement captures global attention, critical questions emerge regarding its leadership, class orientation, and revolutionary potential.

The Spark: Exam Scandals, Judicial Contempt, and the Birth of a Movement
The immediate catalyst for the uprising lies in India's deeply corrupt, highly centralized examination apparatus. On May 3, over 2.3 to 2.5 million high school graduates competed in the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET)—a brutally competitive exam determining entrance into medical colleges across India. For working-class families, NEET represents virtually the only avenue to secure one of approximately 50,000 public medical seats offering affordable tuition, as private institutions charge exorbitant fees far beyond the reach of average workers.

When revelations surfaced that NEET question papers had been leaked and sold by politically connected coaching syndicates, the exam was abruptly cancelled. Years of grueling study, immense emotional stress, and life savings invested by impoverished parents were wiped out in an instant. Tragically, at least 12 young people took their own lives in despair. Opposition sources highlight that over 152 centralized exam leaks have occurred under Modi's regime since 2014 without a single high-profile conviction, exposing systemic rot and state-sanctioned corruption.

"On May 15, Chief Justice Surya Kant sneered from the Supreme Court bench, denouncing unemployed youth protesting exam failures as 'parasites' and 'cockroaches.' Instead of breaking their spirit, the slur ignited a firestorm."

Adding fuel to the fire, Supreme Court Chief Justice Surya Kant openly sneered from the bench on May 15, denouncing India's unemployed youth as "parasites" and "cockroaches." Communications strategist Abhijeet Dipke—a Boston University graduate and former strategist for the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP)—capitalized on the remark by creating a viral satire account on Instagram: the Cockroach Janata Party, parodying the ruling BJP. Within days, the account amassed over 22 million followers, eclipsing every major political party in India and evolving from online satire into a physical mass sit-in at New Delhi's Jantar Mantar.

State Repression and "Sansad Chalo"
The scale of the movement reached a climax on July 20 during the opening of Parliament's Monsoon Session. Tens of thousands of young demonstrators launched a "Sansad Chalo" (March to Parliament), directly defying government bans. In response, the Modi government transformed central Delhi into a militarized zone under what local leaders termed a "marshal raj." Delhi Police and heavily armed paramilitary units—including the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) and Rapid Action Force (RAF)—unleashed ferocious brutality.

Police fired tear gas into peaceful crowds, conducted indiscriminate baton charges (lathi charges), and locked down metro stations to prevent protesters from gathering. Over 200 youth suffered severe injuries, including skull lacerations and broken bones, with a 21-year-old female protester admitted to the ICU. Furthermore, authorities invoked the draconian National Security Act (NSA) of 1980, granting police sweeping powers to detain individuals without trial for up to a year. Environmental activist Sonam Wangchuk engaged in a 26-day hunger strike in solidarity, ending it only as public outrage reached a boiling point.

Despite the violence, the movement's sheer momentum forced the government onto the defensive. In a rare political concession, the administration was pressured into agreeing to a full-fledged Parliamentary discussion via an Adjournment Motion—a procedure unused in the lower house for 25 years. Member of Parliament Dr. John Brittas (CPI-M, Kerala) reported directly from the streets that MPs were forced to physically intercept police vans to free detained students, noting that Modi’s authoritarian hubris had been deeply dented.

Cultural Defiance, "Godi Media," and Subverting the State Narrative
In an interview with Democracy Now!, renowned writer and activist Arundhati Roy highlighted the transformative cultural shift driven by the young protesters. Unlike traditional, rigid political demonstrations, the youth movement is characterized by exuberant joy, satirical humor, music, and street theater. Demonstrators mock police water cannons by asking officers to turn them on to cool off in the Delhi heat, effectively stripping the regime of its fear factor.

Crucially, the youth have completely dismantled the state's media apparatus. For years, corporate-owned news channels—derisively termed "godi media" (laptop/lapdog media)—have served as propaganda outlets for Modi's regime, dominated by oligarchs like Ambani and Adani. When corporate journalists attempt to report from protest sites, students jeer and drive them away.

Instead, young protesters utilize Instagram reels, TikTok, YouTube, and encrypted channels to broadcast raw footage directly to global audiences. By bypassing traditional media, they expose the stark reality behind Modi's carefully crafted international image, turning his speeches into viral objects of ridicule and uniting youth across religious and caste lines—Hindu, Muslim, Sikh, and Christian alike.

Reformism vs. Class Revolution
While the CJP movement has successfully rattled the state, a rigorous socialist analysis reveals structural limits in its current program. The root of this youth explosion is not merely corrupt exam administrators, but the fundamental crisis of Indian capitalism. Official labor statistics reveal India's youth unemployment is at a 45-year high. Over 10 million young workers enter the labor market annually, only to face gig-economy exploitation, underemployment, or absolute poverty. This precarity exists alongside staggering inequality: India's 229 billionaires hoard over $1 trillion in net worth while public education and social services face chronic underfunding.

Supreme Court Interim Orders in CJP Protest Case (July 28, 2026)Bench: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi, and Justice V. Mohana.The Court was hearing a batch of petitions alleging police excesses (and related violence) during student protests over NEET paper leaks and exam irregularities, including the July 20 Parliament march in Delhi and incidents in other states. 

Key Interim DirectionsPreserve evidence: All CCTV footage, drone recordings, body-camera footage, wireless communication logs, and PCR records related to the protests must be preserved. 

Protect digital data: Police authorities must preserve the personal information and digital data of student protesters and ensure it is not brought into the public domain for the time being. No personal data or details of the protesters shall be published. 

No coercive action: No coercive steps shall be taken against students who protested, provided they have no criminal antecedents. (Investigations into registered FIRs may continue, but without coercive measures against eligible students.) 

Release of detainees: All states are directed to release students/children below the age of 18 years who were arrested or detained during the protests and who have no criminal antecedents. Broader directions also cover release of protesting students without criminal antecedents. 

Other Directions and ObservationsNotices issued to the Union of India, NCT of Delhi, and the states of Assam, Bihar, West Bengal, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, and Kerala (Chief Secretaries directed to respond). 

Allegations of excesses (including use of force against students and injuries to police personnel, reported as over 200–250) prima facie warrant a fair, independent, and transparent probe. The Court indicated it may constitute a high-powered committee/SIT (possibly headed by a former judge) after receiving replies from the Centre and states. The probe would address concerns from both sides. 

Evidence materials (including pen drives) were placed on record.
Next hearing: August 3, 2026.

These are interim measures reported from the hearing (primarily via LiveLaw updates and consistent coverage in other outlets). Full written order details may follow. The protection explicitly does not extend to persons with criminal antecedents.

Key Interim DirectionsPreserve evidence: All CCTV footage, drone recordings, body-camera footage, wireless communication logs, and PCR records related to the protests must be preserved. Protect digital data: Police authorities must preserve the personal information and digital data of student protesters and ensure it is not brought into the public domain for the time being. No personal data or details of the protesters shall be published. No coercive action: No coercive steps shall be taken against students who protested, provided they have no criminal antecedents. (Investigations into registered FIRs may continue, but without coercive measures against eligible students.) Release of detainees: All states are directed to release students/children below the age of 18 years who were arrested or detained during the protests and who have no criminal antecedents. Broader directions also cover release of protesting students without criminal antecedents. Other Directions and ObservationsNotices issued to the Union of India, NCT of Delhi, and the states of Assam, Bihar, West Bengal, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, and Kerala (Chief Secretaries directed to respond). Allegations of excesses (including use of force against students and injuries to police personnel, reported as over 200–250) prima facie warrant a fair, independent, and transparent probe. The Court indicated it may constitute a high-powered committee/SIT (possibly headed by a former judge) after receiving replies from the Centre and states. The probe would address concerns from both sides. Evidence materials (including pen drives) were placed on record. Next hearing: August 3, 2026. These are interim measures reported from the hearing (primarily via LiveLaw updates and consistent coverage in other outlets). Full written order details may follow. The protection explicitly does not extend to persons with criminal antecedents.

🚨 Supreme Court Issues Interim Directions on Student Protest Cases

On 28 July 2026, a Supreme Court bench comprising CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi, and Justice V. Mohana heard a batch of petitions concerning alleged police excesses and counter-allegations of injuries to police during the recent student protests over exam irregularities and paper leaks, including the Jantar Mantar demonstrations associated with the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP).

⚖️ Key observations by the Court:
• Peaceful protest is a constitutional right and the demonstrations were initially intended to remain peaceful.
• Violence during protests may sometimes be caused by "uninvited guests" or infiltrators, and not necessarily by the original protesters.
• The Court also noted that petitions have been filed on behalf of injured police personnel, making it clear that allegations from both sides require impartial examination.
• The bench found a prima facie case for an independent and fair investigation into the allegations.

📌 Possible SIT
The Court indicated that it may constitute a Special Investigation Team (SIT) headed by a former Supreme Court judge and sought responses from:

- Union Government
- Delhi Government (NCT)
- Assam
- Bihar
- West Bengal
- Uttar Pradesh
- Madhya Pradesh
- Maharashtra
- Kerala

🗓️ Next hearing: 3 August 2026

✅ Interim Directions
• Release all students arrested or detained for participating in the protests if they have no criminal antecedents.
• No coercive action against such students during the pendency of the matter.
• Preserve all relevant evidence, including CCTV footage, drone recordings, body-worn camera footage, wireless communications, PCR logs, and other records.
• Preserve protesters' personal information and digital data, and ensure it is not made public for the time being.
• The Court also emphasized revisiting protocols on handling demonstrations, reaffirming the principle of graduated use of force and stressing that mere participation in a protest does not justify excessive force.

⚠️ Important Clarification
Some posts on social media are portraying this as blanket protection for all protesters. That is not what the Court said.

The protection applies to students with no criminal antecedents, while any allegations of criminal conduct will still be investigated through due process and evidence. The Court's emphasis was on protecting peaceful protest while ensuring accountability wherever criminal acts are established.

This matter arises from the student protests over exam irregularities and paper leaks, including the NEET controversy, which triggered nationwide demonstrations and significant political fallout.

Future Move of CJP  

Now CJP has secured one resignation. That result has changed the incentives for them for future action.   

They tested an emotional issue, created visible pressure, and extracted a concession. When a method works, it is usually repeated and refined.  

If you analyse the movement The most likely approach from here is for them to look for the next issue that can be mobilised quickly and keep the government reactive.  

Some of the possible targets are:   

1. Another student-related failure  This remains the highest-probability path. Any fresh controversy in competitive exams (JEE, CUET, state exams), scholarship delays, fee hikes, or admission counselling glitches can be framed the same way as NEET. The template already exists: emotional stakes, large affected group, easy moral framing.  

2. Nicobar Island project  This can be positioned as an environmental and tribal rights issue. Large infrastructure in a sensitive zone offers a long campaign runway and multiple angles for sustained protest.  

3. AI Data Centers  These can be attacked on land use, water consumption, energy demand, and weak local job creation. For a generation already anxious about employment, the claim that such projects serve corporations more than citizens has natural appeal.  

In each case the method stays consistent: choose an issue with moral clarity, mobilise fast, amplify through media, and raise demands beyond easy concessions.  The first probe worked. 

The next phase will test whether the same playbook can extract a higher political cost.

OF THE COCKROACH, THE SWEET (PEREMENDE) AND THE HYENA

Never underestimate the power of an insult. Sometimes the people you intend to demean take the insult, wear it as a badge of honour, and turn it against you.

Three stories — two from Kenya and one from India — illustrate this rather well: the cockroach, the peremende and the hyena.

THE COCKROACH — INDIA

India’s Education Minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, resigned on 25 July 2026 after weeks of protests over alleged examination irregularities, particularly the leakage of the NEET-UG examination used for admission to medical and other health-professional courses.

But one of the fascinating aspects of the protests is their name: the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP).

The story appears to have begun in May 2026 following remarks by a Supreme Court judge that were widely interpreted online as comparing unemployed or protesting young people to “cockroaches”. The Court subsequently clarified that the remarks had been taken out of context.

But by then, the cockroach had escaped.

Instead of running away from the derogatory label, young Indians appropriated it.

A satirical idea emerged online: if they were cockroaches, then perhaps they needed a Cockroach Janta Party.

The satire rapidly developed into a youth movement. When the NEET-UG examination controversy erupted, the CJP made it one of its major causes, demanding accountability and the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

What began partly as internet satire became demonstrations, sit-ins and other forms of protest.

And eventually, the Minister resigned.

The cockroach had bitten back.

THE SWEET (PEREMENDE) — KENYA

We have seen something remarkably similar before in Kenya.

In 2012, Kenyan doctors were engaged in industrial action over their terms and conditions of service.

During the dispute, then Medical Services Minister Prof Peter Anyang’ Nyong’o was reported to have characterised the doctors as sulking children crying for peremende — sweets.

It was intended as a dismissive description. The doctors did something clever.They took the insult and owned it.

And so was born the #PeremendeMovement.

Doctors went online explaining exactly which “sweets” they wanted: adequate staffing, equipment, medicines, better working conditions and implementation of agreements reached with government.

Social media became an important part of the industrial action.

Instead of weakening the doctors, the peremende label gave their campaign an identity.

The strike eventually ended with a return-to-work agreement under which the government agreed to honour commitments previously made to doctors.

The sweet had become bitter for those who had coined the description.

THE HYENA (HITI) — KENYA, 2026

Fast-forward to July 2026.

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale has found himself at the centre of controversy following remarks made partly in Somali during a public event in Lafey, Mandera.

At the heart of the dispute is a Somali proverb involving the waraabe — the hyena.

Duale has argued that he was using a traditional Somali proverb about the difficulty of abandoning an entrenched habit. His critics, however, interpreted his wider remarks as referring derogatorily to the Kikuyu community.

The reaction has been swift.

The National Cohesion and Integration Commission has opened investigations into complaints concerning the remarks. Political leaders have demanded an apology.

But something else is happening.

Some Kikuyus on social media have begun appropriating the hyena.

Instead of rejecting the label, they are making jokes about it, producing memes and videos and turning the animal into a symbol of resilience, organisation and collective strength.

The intended insult — or perceived insult — is acquiring a completely different meaning in the hands of those to whom it was allegedly directed.

It sounds strangely familiar.

Cockroach.

Peremende.

Hyena.

Different countries. Different circumstances. Different generations.

But there is a common lesson.

BE CAREFUL WHAT YOU CALL PEOPLE

History is full of examples of derogatory labels being appropriated by the very people they were intended to diminish.

Once that happens, the person who coined the insult loses control of its meaning.

An insult can give a previously scattered group a common identity.
- A joke can become a hashtag.
- A hashtag can become a movement.
- A movement can become political organisation.
- And political organisation can have consequences.

In India, what started as the satirical Cockroach Janta Party became part of a protest movement powerful enough to place enormous pressure on the government and culminate in the resignation of an Education Minister.

In Kenya in 2012, doctors transformed peremende from a dismissive description into the identity of a highly visible campaign during their industrial action.

And now, in 2026, we are watching the word fisi acquire a new political meaning almost in real time.

Whether the current fisi phenomenon disappears as another social-media joke or develops into something politically significant remains to be seen.

But politicians would do well to remember one thing:
- Never give an aggrieved population a name around which it can organise.
- You may intend it as an insult.
- They may turn it into their identity.
- And sometimes, that identity becomes a movement.

Time will tell what becomes of the hyena.
